stories.headline: Second attempt to tranquilise wild tusker Chakkakompan underway in Chinnakkanal: Keralam Forest Minister
stories.deck: Shibu Baby John says the mission, which began on Wednesday, had to be called off in the evening due to adverse weather conditions. The elephant was located again on Thursday morning in a cardamom plantation, and Forest dept team is monitoring its movements to determine if it will enter targeted area
stories.bodyText:
Keralam Forest Minister Shibu Baby John said the second attempt to tranquilise and radio-collar wild elephant Chakkakompan was underway at Chinnakkanal in Idukki on Thursday.
The ongoing efforts would depend on the animal’s movement and prevailing weather conditions, he told mediapersons in Thiruvananthapuram.
The Minister said the mission, which began on Wednesday, had to be called off in the evening due to adverse weather conditions. The elephant was located again on Thursday morning in a cardamom plantation, and the forest team was closely monitoring its movements to determine whether it would enter the targeted area. If it moves into the designated location, a second attempt will be made, he said.
Explaining the failure behind the initial tranquilisation attempt, the Minister said a tranquiliser dart had been fired, but was later found to have fallen off.
Stressing that there was no need to rush the operation, he pointed out that similar missions had taken up to 19 days in the past. The objective was to complete the mission without causing unnecessary stress to the elephant while ensuring the safety of forest personnel. Instructions have been issued to undertake the operation in a manner that would protect both the animal and the people involved, Mr. John said.
Need for caution
Describing Chakkakompan as “an exceptionally strong and intelligent elephant”, the Minister said its behaviour during Wednesday’s operation highlighted the need for caution. “Although the elephant was familiar with human settlements, its reaction to encountering a group of people was different from what was expected. This made it important for the team to proceed scientifically and avoid unnecessary confrontation,” he added.
He also pointed out that the primary objective of the mission is to fit Chakkakompan with a radio collar and monitor its movements. At present, Forest personnel are tracking the elephant by following it from behind. Once the radio collar is fitted, officials will be able to track its movements remotely, identify the direction in which it is travelling and issue timely alerts to people in vulnerable areas.
Besides, the radio collar would help prevent unexpected encounters between the elephant and people, particularly when it moves through roads and human settlements. Such encounters could lead to accidents, and advance information about the elephant’s movements would enable authorities to alert residents and take preventive measures.
The Minister also maintained the mission was being carried out strictly in accordance with the Standard Operating Procedure (SOP), which has received approval from the High Court.

stories.headline: 'Good luck more than anything': John Wright on discovering a young Jasprit Bumrah
stories.bodyText:
Jasprit Bumrah (L) and John Wright.
Credit: PTI Phoro/X
Christchurch: An image that went viral earlier this month was when former Mumbai Indians’ head coach John Wright caught up with his greatest discovery Jasprit Bumrah during the game between India A and New Zealand A in Lincoln, a suburb southwest of Christchurch.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
It was Wright who spotted Bumrah first duringight a Syed Mushtaq Ali T20 Trophy game between Gujarat and Mumbai in Motera while on a scouting programme in 2013, and after a chat with Parthiv Patel he immediately recommended the MI management to rope in the then 19-year-old. The pacer with a gingerly run-up and unique slingy action has now gone on to become one of the best all-format bowlers in the world. And Bumrah still shares a strong bond with the man who opened the window of opportunity for him.
“Oh, well, it was good luck more than anything,” gushed Wright when quizzed about the meeting on Wednesday. The New Zealand great, India’s first-ever foreign coach between November 2000 and April 2005, said he spotted something special the moment he saw Bumrah.
“It was 2013 and I’d just got the opportunity to coach the Mumbai Indians with Anil Kumble. So I went up to the West Zone, for the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy. And there were two games going on at that stage and I watched both. Then I wandered back to the game between Mumbai and Gujarat. It was only about six or seven overs to go.
“Mumbai were going to win. They only had a few runs to get. But there was this kid who bowled from that end. He ran in and I watched him bowl an over and they were all yorkers. He had a bit of pace because one of them hit the bowler's footmarks and the ball took off and went for four byes. I thought, wow, the kid's got a bit of pace too. So I hung around and watched the other over.
“Then he came on again and bowled another over. And he bowled another six yorkers. That's all he tried to bowl. So at the end of the game I wandered over to Parthiv Patel, who's a judge that I really respect. He was captain of Gujarat. I said ‘who's that bloke there?’ Parthiv gave him a very positive recommendation.
Wright immediately dialled Rahul Sanghvi, Director of Cricket at Mumbai Indians, and ensured Bumrah was signed before the auction. The rest, as they say, is history with Bumrah instrumental in MI winning five IPL crowns as well as two T20 World Cups for India.
Wright said the moment batting great Sachin Tendulkar spoke highly of Bumrah he knew he’d made the right call.
“He (Bumrah) was always special. When we signed him, we went to RCB. It was our first game and we had nets. I made him bowl to Sachin in the first nets we had. And at the end of the nets, Sachin came over to me and said ‘Who's that over there?’ And I said ‘Oh, that's a young lad called Bumrah.’ He said ‘Oh John, he’s very hard to pick up. That's when I did a jig for joy.”
“You can pick someone and provide an opportunity. But then it's really up to the individual cricketer of what they’re going to make of that opportunity. And Jasprit, from my experience, is intelligent. I think he's quite humble. He's got an aptitude to learn. The most unique thing about him is the action. He's made the most of his opportunities. Someone would have found him at some stage. But I’m thrilled for the guy because he's been a great bowler and is a great bowler.”
Talent scouting is huge in IPL nowadays given the amount of cricket that takes place, not just in India but across the world too. When asked what attributes a good scout needs to have, Wright felt intuition is very important. “It probably boils down to an eye. I'm not too sure, but for me personally, sometimes it can just be one shot or the way the ball bounces off the wicket. And then it arouses interest where you see something that's a little bit different or maybe a bit special or something.
“With Hardik (Pandya) it was one shot, Bumrah we've talked about. The really good ones stand out. Sometimes it's a little bit of luck. I don't think it's an exact art. Sometimes you just hope you're lucky. But for me, I always like people who do well when the pressure is on. And I particularly notice more in the game situation than anything else. People who can perform when maybe the game's on the line will make a difference. Because sometimes that means that the temperament might be all right. And hunger is quite a big factor too.”
Wright was all praise for IPL for constantly providing opportunities for domestic talents to make it big. “What I do think is fantastic with IPL is that everyone is now looking for the best talent. And that's just so great for kids growing up in India. And knowing that if they can get an opportunity to play at first-class level, there's going to be a whole lot of people looking at them to maybe give them that opportunity which can make a huge difference to their lives personally and their family. I think that that's one of the great things that's happened with IPL. You know there's no traditional barriers anymore. Everyone's after talent and after someone that can make their team the best,” concluded Wright.

stories.headline: Kerala HC allows pregnancy termination of minor rape victim despite serious risks in procedure
stories.bodyText:
Kerala HC allows pregnancy termination of minor rape victim despite serious risks in procedure
The court said that if the baby does not survive, the hospital shall preserve tissues and blood samples of the foetus for necessary medical tests, including DNA, fingerprinting, and mapping, since an FIR has been registered.
Kochi: The Kerala High Court has permitted a minor rape victim to undergo medical termination of her over 27-week pregnancy, even though the medical board said the procedure could result in her death, as the girl was unwilling to continue until the 32 weeks suggested by the doctors.
Justice Harisankar V Menon said that since the victim is a minor who is pursuing her studies, "her wish also requires to be given utmost sanctity".
"Therefore, taking note of the factual and legal position, I am of the opinion that the prayer made by the petitioner requires to be immediately allowed," the court said.
The medical board constituted on the court's orders had examined the girl and given a report stating that terminating the pregnancy at the current stage carried the increased risk of excessive haemorrhage, retained placenta, uterine rupture, premature rupture of membranes, high chances of infection, and anaesthetic risks including cardiac arrest and even death of the mother.
The board had also opined that the procedure could adversely affect the girl's future pregnancies too.
As the girl was unwilling to continue with the pregnancy, the court ordered the state government to make the arrangements for the termination of the pregnancy and to carry out the same without any delay after getting an undertaking from the victim regarding her willingness for the procedure.
"If, in the event, the child (baby) survives the termination of the pregnancy, the state shall provide appropriate measures and standard neonatal care," the court said.
It also said that if the victim did not want the baby, she shall unconditionally surrender the infant to a childcare institution or specialised adoption agency for being placed in adoption.
The court said that if the baby does not survive, the hospital shall preserve tissues and blood samples of the foetus for necessary medical tests, including DNA, fingerprinting, and mapping, since an FIR has been registered.

stories.headline: 18 years after 26/11 terror attack, how has India secured its coastal frontier
stories.deck: After the 2008 Mumbai attacks, India's maritime security framework underwent significant changes to address vulnerabilities. The navy assumed leadership in coordinating overall maritime security alongside the coast guard and state marine police. Integrated surveillance systems were established to track suspicious activities and improve information sharing. Recent exercises proved that while…
stories.bodyText:
Eighteen years after the November 2008 Mumbai attacks exposed serious gaps in maritime surveillance and intelligence coordination. The 26/11 attacks saw 10 
Lashkar-e-Taiba
 terrorists reach Mumbai by sea after commandeering the fishing trawler Kuber. The terrorists had travelled from Karachi, killed the trawler's captain and used inflatable boats to land undetected. The attacks, which killed 166 people, led to a fundamental rethink. The navy became the lead agency for overall maritime security, including coastal and offshore security. The coast guard was made responsible for coordinating coastal security in territorial waters, while state marine police continued to handle shallow coastal areas.
In order to have better response and coordination, the navy has regularly holds exercises such as Sea Vigil-26, which strengthens the coastal security architecture. The fifth edition of the nationwide exercise, held from November 11 to 19, tested the preparedness of the navy, coast guard, coastal police, customs and other agencies responsible for securing the coastline and the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ). Fishing and coastal communities also took part, in recognition of their role in spotting suspicious activity at sea.
A key change has been an integrated surveillance and information-sharing network, with the Information Management and Analysis Centre (IMAC), set up in Gurugram in 2014 and run by the navy. The IMAC collects, analyses and disseminates maritime security information. The centre draws on coastal radars, Automatic Identification System (AIS) transmissions, shipping databases, intelligence inputs and international arrangements to build a common operational picture and flag vessels behaving suspiciously. The Information Fusion Centre for the Indian Ocean Region, established in 2018, extends this by exchanging information with regional and international partners.
The coastal surveillance network is another pillar, according to the coast guard, it has static sensor stations with radars, AIS, day-and-night cameras and meteorological systems at 46 locations along the coast and islands. Its second phase envisages 38 more radar stations and eight mobile surveillance systems. The coast guard also carries out regular boardings to verify the identity and registration documents of fishing vessels and the people on board.
Yet surveillance depends on being able to track a vast number of small boats, as many fishing vessels do not carry AIS transponders, which leaves gaps in the maritime picture. A substantial share of the fishing fleet consisted of smaller vessels that don't have transponders. The government has since tried to expand tracking and distress-alert equipment among fishermen, but ensuring that small boats are registered, identifiable and connected to the network remains a challenge. AIS also cannot detect vessels that do not transmit or deliberately switch off their equipment.
Sea Vigil-26 tested some of these weaknesses, this edition simulated terrorists commandeering fishing boats to reach the shore, attacks on coastal installations, merchant ship hijackings near port limits and drone attacks. Joint audit teams inspected fish landing centres, coastal police stations, ports and other critical sites. It was the first edition since Operation Sindoor and the first since the coastline was officially remeasured at 11,098 km, up from 7,516 km.
The threat has also evolved since 2008, while infiltration through fishing boats remains possible, but agencies must now reckon with unmanned surface vessels, underwater drones, commercial aerial drones, encrypted communications and potential strikes on ports, offshore energy assets and other critical infrastructure. Recent conflicts have shown how cheap unmanned platforms can threaten high-value targets. Coastal defence will therefore need sensors that cover the surface, air and underwater domains, not just conventional vessel tracking.
Coordination is the other challenge as the framework involves the navy, coast guard, marine police, intelligence agencies, port authorities, customs and several central and state departments. IMAC and the radar network have improved information sharing, but their value depends on how quickly information reaches the agency that must respond. Coastal police stations, in turn, need adequate boats, communication equipment and trained personnel to work alongside central forces.

briefs.headline: U.S. announces new 25% tariffs on India, second-highest in the 14 countries against which action has been taken
briefs.deck: The order by the U.S. Trade Representative also opens the door for a lower 17% tariff if India and the U.S. sign a trade deal
briefs.bodyText:
The U.S. government on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) announced a tariff of 25% on goods imported from India in response to India’s “unreasonable acts, policies, and practices” that “burden or restrict U.S. commerce”. This is the second-highest tariff among the 14 economies against which the latest action has been taken, second only to the 35% tariff levied on Vietnam.
However, the order by the office of the U.S. Trade Representative (USTR) also said that, should the U.S. and India reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, the tariff imposed on India could drop to 17%.
Further, while it says that the 25% tariffs would be net of existing tariffs levied on India, meaning they will not add to the 10% already in effect, the order also said that it remained for the USTR to decide whether these new tariffs would be adjusted keeping in mind those other tariffs.
The Indian government said it has taken note of the actions by the USTR and that its notice is currently under examination.
“India engaged constructively throughout this investigation,” the statement by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry said. “In response to the Notice of Initiation and in subsequent proceedings, the Department of Commerce stated that India does not have structural excess capacity in any sector.”
“India and the United States are engaged in negotiations for a Bilateral Trade Agreement,” it added. “It has been India’s position that any trade-related concerns should be addressed within the framework of these negotiations. Government of India remains committed to working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement, as announced on 2nd February 2026 and in accordance with the Joint Statement issued on 7th February 2026.”
Tariff pressure
The USTR had in March launched two separate investigations into American trade partners, including India, under Section 301 of the U.S. Trade Act. The first investigation related to forced labour resulted in a tariff of 10% levied on India. The new tariffs announced on Wednesday are a result of the second investigation into structural excess capacity.
Apart from this, the U.S. also levies a tariff of 50% on imports of aluminium and steel from all countries under Section 232 of its Trade Expansion Act. The new tariffs will not be added to these. Under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, the U.S. government is also empowered to levy a tariff of up to 100% on countries, including India, that import large quantities of Russian oil. This tariff has been temporarily paused by U.S. President Donald Trump.
In its report on India, the USTR concluded that India’s acts, policies, and practices “create, sustain, or contribute to structural excess capacity” that burden or restrict U.S. commerce by harming U.S. producers and exporters through unfair competition and reduced commercial opportunities; harm the U.S. economy due to lost exports, trade deficits, and a diminished manufacturing sector; and create economic security risks for the U.S.
“The Trade Representative proposes that appropriate action to obtain the elimination of the acts, policies, and practices would include applying tariffs of up to 25% on all goods of India, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, with exemptions for certain goods,” the order by the USTR said.
Way out
However, the order also says that the USTR further proposes to consider whether the additional duties applied should be adjusted to account for duties applied under other existing Section 301 actions, duties applied under Section 232, “or were India to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with the United States that is responsive to the determinations in this investigation into the acts, policies, and practices of India, a tariff rate of 17%”.
The 25% tariffs are higher than those levied on Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, Taiwan, the European Union (15% each), Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand (18% each), Bangladesh, Cambodia, China, and Singapore (up to 20% each).
Only Vietnam faces a tariff of 35%, higher than that for India, but even that stands to be reduced to 20% if it signs a trade deal with the U.S.
India and the U.S. issued a joint statement in February 2026 announcing a framework for an interim deal on trade under which the U.S. would levy a tariff of 18% on imports from India. That deal is yet to be finalised, however.
Should it be finalised and tariffs settle at 17%, this would give India a comparative advantage over its competitors.

briefs.headline: CJP’s Saurav Das to file criminal complaints against social media handles over passport leak
briefs.deck: The CJP co-convenor alleged targeted harassment as his passport details were circulated online after he was stopped from boarding London-bound flight over discrepancies flagged by Chennai passport office
briefs.bodyText:
Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) co-convenor Saurav Das has said he will lodge criminal complaints against every social media handle involved in circulating his passport online, alleging a sustained campaign of targeted harassment, after images of the travel document were leaked on social media platforms following his being stopped from boarding a London-bound flight.
In a post on X, Mr. Das accused several BJP-aligned social media handles of circulating his passport. He questioned how a citizen’s personal travel document could be accessed and shared publicly. He also sought clarification from the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), asking whether the leaking of citizens’ passport details had become routine and whether doxxing had been legalised in the country.
“I shall be filing a criminal complaint with the relevant authorities against every social media handle involved in circulating my passport,” he said, adding that he was documenting every instance of harassment and the handles involved.
Mr. Das alleged that the circulation of his passport was the latest in a series of incidents in which his personal information had been made public. He claimed that a social media account had earlier leaked his Delhi residential address, after which YouTubers allegedly entered his house while he was away from the city. He also accused social media users of circulating fabricated accounts of his family life and a morphed photograph of him.
Citing the pattern of alleged harassment, he said he had specifically requested the SEM Court to ensure that his rent agreement was not leaked.
The latest controversy comes two days after Mr. Das was stopped from boarding a London-bound flight at the Indira Gandhi International Airport (IGI) in Delhi on the intervening night of November 23 and 24. He was scheduled to attend engagements at the Oxford Union and other institutions in the United Kingdom, including the University of Cambridge, the London School of Economics and the University of Edinburgh.
Mr. Das was stopped at the immigration counter after the Regional Passport Office (RPO), Chennai, issued him a show-cause notice over discrepancies in the place of birth mentioned in his passport application and other identity documents.
The notice, issued on November 23 and emailed to him at around 7.30 p.m., stated that the RPO had received inputs that the particulars relating to his place of birth in his passport application, submitted on August 8, 2019, were incorrect. It also alleged that the passport, issued on August 21, 2019, had been obtained through material suppression of facts.
The RPO gave him seven days to submit an explanation along with supporting documents and warned that failure to provide a satisfactory response could result in the impounding of his passport under Section 10(3)(b) of the Passports Act, 1967. He was also advised not to use the passport until he submitted his response.
The MEA on Wednesday confirmed that the notice had been issued by the Chennai RPO following inputs from law enforcement authorities. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the notice sought clarification regarding Mr. Das’s place of birth and that he had been advised not to use the passport until he submitted his response.
Meanwhile, Mr. Das has approached the Delhi High Court challenging the action that prevented him from travelling abroad. His counsel submitted that no formal order or lookout circular restricting his travel had been shown to him at the airport. The court listed the matter for hearing on November 26.

briefs.headline: 'Perhaps it will be good': NCP-SP softening stance on Delimitation Bill? Supriya Sule hints at support
briefs.bodyText:
In a rare show of support, NCP (SP) MP Supriya Sule on Wednesday called for the Delimitation Bill to be introduced in the Parliament before there is a debate on its provisions, claiming that could turn out to be good for the country.
She said that the entire text of the bill should be made available to legislators before they take a decision on the proposed Constitution amendment.
"Let the bill be introduced first; let us have the full bill in our hands. Once we have it, we can discuss it, and perhaps it will turn out to be a good one," she said, adding that the ruling party and the opposition have worked together on several occasions in view of national interest.
Earlier, Sule had indicated that her party is willing to support the delimitation bill if all states get a uniform 50 per cent rise in seats.
This comes amid reports that the government is planning to call for a special session of the Parliament to pass the Delimitation Bill, which also includes provisions for 33 per cent women's reservation in both General and Assembly elections.
The proposed amendment aims to increase the strength of the Lok Sabha to 850 seats. The BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) has maintained that delimitation is necessary to reflect new census data and facilitate the implementation of women's reservation. However, the opposition, led by the Congress, has demanded that the 33 per cent quota be implemented in the existing 543-member Lok Sabha, opposing its linkage to delimitation.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on April 16 to increase the strength of the Lower House to 850 seats and expedite the implementation of the Women's Reservation Bill, passed in 2023.
However, the bill failed to secure the required special two-thirds majority of members present and voting in Parliament and was consequently not passed.

briefs.headline: Constitution soul of India, greatest weapon against injustice: Congress
briefs.bodyText:
In a post on X on Constitution Day, the leader of opposition in Lok Sabha (LoP) said it is the foundation of our democracy and a weapon against injustice.
"India's Constitution is not just a book; it is the soul of the nation. It is a shield for every citizen's dignity, the strength of every voice, a guardian of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity," he said in his post, further calling it "our greatest weapon against injustice".
"On Constitution Day, I renew my pledge; we will defend it under all circumstances and keep fighting for every Indian's rights. Long live the Constitution, long live India!" the LoP asserted.
भारत का संविधान सिर्फ़ एक किताब नहीं - देश की आत्मा है। ये हर नागरिक की गरिमा का कवच है, हर आवाज़ की ताक़त है - न्याय, स्वतंत्रता, समानता और भाईचारे का रक्षक। यही हमारे लोकतंत्र की नींव है, और अन्याय के ख़िलाफ़ हमारा सबसे बड़ा हथियार। संविधान दिवस पर संकल्प दोहराता हूँ - हम हर… pic.twitter.com/mWVPYodoCj
Congress chief Mallikarjun Kharge also gave his best wishes to fellow citizens on Constitution Day and reaffirmed his pledge to save it along with democracy.
"Political democracy cannot survive unless there is social democracy at its foundation," he said in a post on X, quoting Dr B R Ambedkar.
"Heartfelt wishes to all fellow citizens on Constitution Day," he said while giving salutations to Mahatma Gandhi, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose, Maulana Azad, Dr Rajendra Prasad, Sarojini Naidu, Ambedkar and all the great national leaders who laid the foundation of modern India.
"Today, protecting the Constitution's core ideals -- justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, secularism and socialism -- is our greatest national responsibility. Let us renew our pledge to protect the Constitution and democracy and preserve the country's unity, integrity, and harmony. Victory to India. Victory to the Constitution," Kharge said in his post.
The Congress has organised protests against "vote chori" across the country to mark the day.

briefs.headline: ‘Meta BJP ka Beta’: Zuckerberg posters in RSS attire emerge in Bengaluru as Youth Congress protests
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Mark Zuckerberg
 has got a political makeover in Bengaluru, with the Karnataka Pradesh Youth Congress putting up posters depicting the Meta chief executive in Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (
RSS
) attire and branding him “Mark 
BJP
berg”. The satirical posters of Zuckerberg come as the Youth Congress accuse the social media giant of favouring the ruling BJP.
The campaign, led by Karnataka Pradesh Youth Congress Committee president H S Manjunath Gowda, features the slogan “Meta BJP ka Beta” and has appeared at several locations across the city, including Sadahalli Gate on New Airport Road, near the toll plaza and in Chikkajala.
The Youth Congress shared photographs of the posters on X, saying: “BJP ka Beta Meta enters to Namma Bengaluru! Mark Bjpberg is getting famous than Meta.”
The campaign is part of a wider confrontation between the Congress and Meta over allegations that the company selectively restricts opposition voices while failing to act impartially on fake news, hate speech and user privacy.
The party has accused Meta of applying its content moderation policies unevenly across political groups and questioned whether its platforms are being used in ways that undermine democratic values. 
Meta has maintained that it follows Indian law and remains politically neutral.
The poster campaign follows protests by Indian Youth Congress workers at Meta offices in Hyderabad, Mumbai and Gurugram over alleged restrictions on the social media accounts of Congress leaders and other opposition figures.
In a post dated November 21, the Youth Congress alleged that Meta had withheld the Instagram accounts of Indian Youth Congress president and a national in-charge at the BJP’s behest. It claimed the accounts were restored within 15 minutes of protests outside the company’s offices, and questioned whether the timing was a “coincidence”.
The organisation issued a seven-day ultimatum to Meta, demanding that it remove restrictions on accounts belonging to opposition leaders, journalists and content creators.
“Must Indians visit your offices every time you silence them?” it asked.
The protests have since spread to several cities, including Delhi, Kolkata, Patna and Bengaluru, with demonstrators demanding that Meta explain how its algorithms decide which political posts are restricted and restore accounts taken down on government orders.
Amid the escalating row, Meta officials met Congress leaders at the party headquarters in New Delhi on Tuesday. Meta executives Aman Jain and Natasha Jog met AICC social media department chairperson Supriya Shrinate, following a request from the company.
Congress leaders raised concerns over what they described as growing restrictions on opposition accounts and posts, alleging that Meta was interfering in Indian politics and favouring the BJP.
Meta officials said the company was bound by Indian laws and had to remove posts within three hours of a government request. They reiterated that the company was politically neutral and made no commitments to the Congress, people familiar with the discussions said.

The meeting also came after Meta executives expressed concern over protests targeting the company’s offices and posters featuring Zuckerberg in RSS attire.
The dispute has drawn attention to the scale of content restrictions imposed by Meta in India. The company restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts under local laws in the first half of 2026, compared with around 70,000 during the whole of 2025, according to company disclosures cited by Reuters.
Meta has attributed the increase to amendments to India’s information technology rules, which require platforms to remove content more quickly and proactively. The rising number of restrictions has renewed concerns over freedom of expression as the government steps up requests for online content removal.

briefs.headline: Nepal flash floods: Kathmandu begins process to declare 213 missing Indians presumed dead
briefs.deck: Inviting objections or concerns, the Embassy said concerned family members could contact it via eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com or +9779851316807
briefs.bodyText:
The Nepal government has begun the process of presumption and declaration of death for 213 Indian nationals who remain missing since the flash floods in August this year, the Indian Embassy in Nepal said.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) has published a list of the 213 missing Indian nationals for presumption and declaration of death on its website, the Embassy said in a press release on Wednesday (November 25, 2026).
The NDRRMA has invited objections for additions, deletions or amendments in the details contained in the list.
In case the family members of persons who remain missing have any concerns, objections or proposed changes regarding this list, they can contact the Indian Embassy before December 2, it said. They could contact via the email address eoikathmandufloodsupport@gmail.com or mobile phone number +9779851316807.
The Nepal government will finalise the list and formally issue the declaration of death after completing the process of seeking comments or amendments.
The Embassy will then begin obtaining death certificates for these individuals from local authorities in Nepal.
Nepal’s flash floods: How can communities rebuild after a disaster?
During this process, the Embassy may seek additional details and documents from family members of the missing persons, and will provide a suitable update in the coming days, it said.
The August 26 flash floods that took place in the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi river system killed at least 1,453 people, and left more than 5,000 missing, according to the NDRRMA.

briefs.headline: How Alexandr Wang and Mark Zuckerberg plan Meta's AI launches, research and hardware
briefs.deck: Meta AI head Alexandr Wang and CEO Mark Zuckerberg frequently discuss both immediate and long-term strategies for AI. They focus on launching products like Muse while also planning research roadmaps over several months. Their multiyear plans include developing custom AI chips and building data centers to improve computing infrastructure. Muse, a personal AI agent, is designed to assist users…
briefs.bodyText:
Meta AI head Alexandr Wang says he and CEO 
Mark Zuckerberg
 talk frequently about plans that run from day-to-day product decisions to investments that take years. Wang pointed to Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, as an example of the decisions they make each week as the company rolls out features and expands into new countries.
Speaking on The Eric Newcomer Show, Wang said the pace of the artificial intelligence (AI) industry means the two have to plan across three time scales. The immediate decisions are about what to launch and where. Over the following months, the focus is on what Meta’s AI researchers should work on and how that work is progressing. The multiyear plan covers computing infrastructure, from data centres to chips Meta designs itself.
What Alexandr Wang said about working with Mark Zuckerberg
Asked about working with Zuckerberg, Wang said,
“I mean, we're definitely talking a lot. We're chatting a lot. But I think the AI industry is moving so fast and you have to be able to plan across multiple different time scales.”So there's obviously a lot of week-to-week decisions and day-to-day decisions. And a lot of those, even in relation to Muse, every week we're launching in new countries and we're launching new features and we're trying to map all of that out.But then there's also the somewhat longer term, which is maybe over the month's time scale, which is really the research roadmap. And what does that look like and how are we executing against that?And then there's the multiyear dimension, which is the compute roadmap. And what does that look like, including everywhere from obviously the data centers we're building all the way down to our own chips and the MTIA chips that we're developing.”How Muse and Meta’s own AI chips fit into those plans
Meta launched Muse in the UK on November 23, making it available to adults on iOS, Android, the web and WhatsApp. The agent runs on Muse Spark, the first model from Meta Superintelligence Labs. It can work across connected apps and websites to carry out tasks and asks for approval before taking actions such as sending an email or making a purchase.
On the hardware side, MTIA stands for Meta Training and Inference Accelerator, the company’s family of custom AI chips. In March, Meta said it planned to develop and deploy four new generations of MTIA chips over two years to support workloads including recommendations and generative AI. The chips are one part of the longer-term computing plan Wang described, alongside the data centres that house them.

briefs.headline: India vs New Zealand | 'There's no pattern': Morne Morkel on struggle to pick 20 wickets
briefs.bodyText:
Indian bowling coach Morne Morkel.
Credit: PTI Photo
Christchurch: For two consecutive Tests now, India have had the opposition under the mat but they haven’t been able to enforce a result with both games ending up in draws that has significantly hurt their scoring in the World Test Championship table.
Experience a more refined e-paper today
Although the pitches in both the matches — the first being the Sinhalese Sports Club Ground in Colombo in late August and the second at Basin Reserve in Wellington last week — had flattened out considerably making batting easy and bowling a real hard task, the lack of cutting edge, at times, was visible.
In Colombo, India looked on course for 2-0 whitewash when they reduced Sri Lanka to 229/6 at stumps on the fourth day after asking the hosts to follow-on. Just ahead by 16 runs but only four wickets in hand, Sri Lanka were staring down the barrel but overnight batter Sonal Dinusha scored an unbeaten 133 off 264 balls and forged two key partnerships with Keshara Nuwantha (46, 150b) and Lahiru Kumara (12, 90b) to defy India.
In Wellington, it was Daryl Mitchell (49 n.o., 186b), Tom Blundell (15, 54b) and Glenn Phillips (26 n.o., 126b) who batted with extreme discipline to ensure India didn’t nick the game despite bowling their hearts out on a largely unresponsive surface.
It’s in moments and days like these that teams need a moment of magic or slice of luck to swing the momentum their way and India could find neither. When asked if India’s inability to bowl out sides or the failure to get them out quickly is becoming a matter of concern, bowling coach Morne Morkel said his bowlers tried as hard as they could.
“To be honest with you, there's no pattern sort of standing out. Every Test match, there was a difference, if you do the review, if you look at, you know, the whys that potentially didn’t happen, there's a different thing that pops out. So it's almost like, prepare for one thing, try to make one area a little better,” the South African said on the eve of the second Test starting against New Zealand on Friday.
“So I think that's the beauty about the game. If you look at the week leading up to the last Test match, raining, you know, we saw the wicket, it was a nice amount of grass cover. It looked like it was going to be also a surface that will make a couple of dents, and if those dents get a little bit harder, they create a bit of up and down which we didn't see. Not a lot of balls kept low. There's not a lot of variation off the surface. Like I said, it's been a challenging sort of period that we're also trying to get better at and put our finger on. But I think at the moment things are going the way we would like.”
Will Brar play?
India skipper Shubman Gill, after the opening Test, said the team for the second too will likely be the same XI. When asked if Gurnoor Brar could replace the disappointing Anshul Kamboj, Morkel said it’s up to the team management. “With Gurnoor, there's a lot of excitement about him since he's joined the Indian team with his pace and bounce. I think he's a guy that will be well-suited to the conditions here. We'll see how it goes, and the pitch.
“Gurnoor has been knocking on the door. He's doing all the right things. But, again, the selection for him as a player is something that I can’t (comment). He needs to just make sure he's ready when he gets the opportunity. I think a lot of times, we think we want that opportunity. We want to be close, and as a bowler, you can get distracted. When he gets his opportunity, which is we never know. My job is to make sure he's 100% ready when he gets that opportunity.”

stories.headline: Bengaluru hospital's CPAP machine overheats to 69 degrees, burns 29-week premature baby's nose within 27 hours of birth; consumer court orders hospital to pay Rs 40 lakh for lifelong injuries
stories.deck: In a landmark ruling, a Bengaluru consumer commission has mandated ESIC Medical College and Hospital to pay Rs 40 lakh to a mother after a heart-wrenching incident involving her premature baby. The infant, who suffered devastating burns in the neonatal intensive care unit due to an overheating CPAP machine, now faces lifelong medical challenges. The commission highlighted the hospital's…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A consumer commission in Bengaluru has directed a government medical college and hospital to pay Rs 40 lakh in compensation to the mother of a premature baby girl who suffered severe burns to her nose after a medical device overheated in the hospital's neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) in 2022.
The commission held ESIC Medical College and Hospital in Rajajinagar, its dean, chief medical officer and the then NICU in-charge responsible for medical negligence and deficiency in service. In its November 4 order, the commission, headed by president Syed Anser Kaleem, said the hospital could not avoid liability by blaming a manufacturing defect in the equipment.
The complaint said the woman, a resident of JP Nagar, delivered the baby girl through an emergency caesarean section on August 18, 2022. The child was born at 29 weeks and three days of gestation, weighing 1.22 kg. The newborn was diagnosed with severe Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) and placed on a Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) machine to support her breathing, according to the complaint.
However, about 27 hours after her birth, the machine's thermostat and humidifier allegedly malfunctioned, causing its temperature to rise to between 52 and 69 degrees Celsius. 
Flames and fumes reportedly emerged from the equipment. The baby suffered severe burns to her nose and was shifted to Narayana Hrudayalaya on August 19, 2022, for advanced treatment. She remained under treatment for 90 days, the order said.
The mother told the commission that the injuries had left the child, now two years old, with permanent nasal disfigurement and severe black scarring. She said the girl would require extensive medical interventions in the future, including nasal debridement and planned nasal reconstruction. The child had also developed permanent patchy hair loss in a specific region, the complaint stated.
The hospital, however, argued that the four-year-old CPAP machine was covered by a comprehensive maintenance contract and had been certified as functioning normally during its last preventive maintenance check in March 2022. It contended that the equipment had failed due to a manufacturing defect and that it had provided the necessary treatment and follow-up care, including bearing the expenses of the child's 90-day hospitalisation at Narayana Hrudayalaya.
The hospital also said it had terminated the use of all medical devices manufactured by the company concerned across its facilities and blacklisted the manufacturer, stopping any future procurement of its products. The commission said the hospital had a responsibility to ensure that medical equipment used on a vulnerable newborn was safe and properly monitored. It held that the hospital could not escape liability by attributing the incident to a manufacturing defect.
"For a CPAP machine to overheat to the extent of producing visible flames and fumes inside an infant's nasal passage implies a profound breakdown of active institutional monitoring," it said.
Taking note of the child's permanent injuries and the need for future medical treatment, the commission directed the hospital and the three officials to jointly and severally pay Rs 40 lakh in compensation, along with interest at six per cent per annum from the date of filing the complaint until the amount is realised. The commission said the injuries would have lifelong consequences for the child.
"Any amount of compensation cannot bring back the originality of the child and the child has to suffer lifelong." It also directed that the compensation be deposited in a long-term fixed deposit in a nationalised bank in the minor's name until she attains majority. The mother will be allowed to withdraw the quarterly interest for the child's medical expenses and welfare, the order said.
(With inputs from PTI)

stories.headline: Minister to Greater Bengaluru Authority officers: Have you ever walked on step footpaths?
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: “Have you ever walked on footpaths? You are interested in completing work and claiming bills. You don’t bother to check if the footpaths are usable,” said Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda during a Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) review meeting on Wednesday.
The minister shot multiple, uncomfortable posers to civic officials and engineers, while urging them to rethink how they build pavements for the city. He was surprised at the presence of step pavements — instead of slope pavements — which are least pedestrian friendly.
These searing questions were at the heart of discussions at GBA meeting. Gowda pointed to problems faced by the elderly and the children while navigating pavements. He pulled up civic engineers and officials for constructing step pavements. Flagging footpaths as high as two feet, he asked whether children and senior citizens could use them. “Even healthy adults will avoid such footpaths,” he said, adding people might ask for escalators to access them.
Gowda asked engineers to go for slope footpaths without single or multiple steps, particularly near property gates and driveways. 
On complaints from property owners that pavements are higher than their entrances, the minister countered: “When the road has a slope, is there a rule that stated that the footpath cannot have a slope?” he asked.
He instructed engineers to ensure continuity of footpaths at edges and turning points and install bollards to prevent vehicles from being driven onto pedestrian pathways.
TOI spoke to engineers who maintained that step pavements are usually done on congested roads where pedestrian movement is high. This apart, step pavements would deter two-wheeler riders from riding on pavements, which is a major menace in the city. The minister countered: “If the number of steps are more, then the number of people wanting to use footpaths would reduce. Pay attention to usability too.”
‘Remove Obstacles From Footpaths’
“Footpaths must be raised by 6 inches, but ramps could be provided at places where there are gates, while ensuring the footpath remains continuous. Steps may become inevitable only at intersections if there’s a height difference. The most important thing is to remove obstacles from footpaths,” said Anil Kumar J, retired engineer, Jalahalli West.
“Discussions on making footpaths accessible have been going on for 20 years with little progress. Even when facilities are created for persons with disabilities, people do not cooperate. Even if good footpaths are built, they last only a couple of months. This is a very difficult task,” added P Balaram, International Para Athlete, Jeevanahalli.
“If footpaths are not built at a height, vehicles will ply or park on them. Even drivers trying to overtake will use such footpaths. Our civic sense is at a low. Railings separating footpaths are essential. However, footpaths can be made seamless. Engineers should supervise the work better. At least in Bengaluru, there are efforts to make footpaths accessible,” said Ajay Kumar C, Swayam Jagruthi NGO, Nagarabhavi.
STEP OR SLOPE?Step pavement: This design raises the footpath above the carriageway and relies on vertical drops or concrete steps at driveways, intersections, and level changes. The abrupt height difference creates a physical barrier that keeps vehicles off the walkway and channels rainwater into the roadside storm drain below.
Slope pavement: Also called ramped pavements, these are commonly seen on TenderSURE roads such as Church Street, St Mark’s Road, and Residency Road. At property driveways and junctions, the footpath stays continuous and the slopes allow effortless movement for wheelchairs and luggage. Elderly pedestrians do not have to strain themselves stepping up and down.

stories.headline: This new book explores the ashwath kattes of Bengaluru
stories.deck: Co-authors Kiran Keswani and Suresh Bhagavatula discuss why, given the interdependencies between the religious, social and economic activities, ashwath kattes are a fantastic model of shared spaces
stories.bodyText:
The genesis of The City Beneath the Tree: How Design and Social Interactions Shape Small Public Spaces in Bengaluru, a new book published by Permanent Black delving into the ashwath kattes of Bengaluru, goes back over a decade. “Somewhere in 2015, I went to a volunteer meeting for the Bangalore Tree Festival, where I heard the term ‘ashwath katte’ for the first time,” recalls Bengaluru-based architect and urban designer Kiran Keswani, who has co-authored the book with Suresh Bhagavatula, Professor of Entrepreneurship at IIM Bangalore. “Once we had heard about them, we realised that they were just everywhere,” she says.
They soon realised that ashwath kattes were not only traditional places of worship, but were also active social spaces used by people across generations, including the elderly, office-goers, and mothers with their young children. As someone who works on networks and how they play a role in creating possibilities for people, Suresh also noticed that when people visit kattes to interact , connections leading to trust and reciprocity are created. “Who we spend time with has a great role to play in what we become in life. So, I began thinking about how spaces like this could influence the networks of those who visited the space,” he says.
To explore these spaces further, Suresh and Kiran wrote a joint proposal for the Azim Premji University External Research Grant under the theme ‘Urban Sustainability and Governance ’, which came through for 2018-19. “We began delving deeper into the networks of the people who visited these kattes,” says Suresh.
Using citizen science, they mapped around 100 kattes around Bengaluru, choosing 20 for in-depth research. From an urban design perspective, Kiran says, the study evaluated parameters like spatial organisation, accessibility and walkability. They also used a “name-generator” technique to understand social networks at these spaces better, says Suresh. “Asking people who they interacted with over the last six months helped us analyse the networks at each of these kattes.”
One of the things that these kattes hint at is how much Bengaluru, as a city, has expanded, with the urban centre taking over many villages at the peripheries. “While on one front, Bengaluru is modern with lots of glass and steel, there is also a part where people are hanging on to some of these older traditions of what the neighbourhood was,” says Suresh. For instance, some of these kattes, including the one at Mavalli, serve as sites for the ooru habba, a traditional village festival celebration. “While the village itself is integrated into the urban fabric with its physical boundaries now not visible, the processional path of the once-in-three-years ooru habba still traces the boundary of the village,” says Kiran.
During the course of their research, they made yet another discovery: many of the kattes are located near Mariamman temples. “Since these kattes do have rural origins, and in the past, it was believed that the peepal tree or ashwatha was the embodiment of the deity, the tree was at every corner of the village, meant to protect it from natural disasters or calamities,” she explains.
One more insight that came out of this study was that while there is indeed a religious angle to these kattes, these spaces can be considered a kind of urban commons. “Everybody comes together here, so the “commoning” is the religious, social and economic practices through which people co-manage these spaces,” says Kiran, comparing these spaces to parks, which can also be thought of as commons, but are controlled by the local government. “In that sense, a katte is more a commons than a park, since here the ownership is with the community,” she says.
The book, which they began working on around two-and-a-half years ago, also touches upon the relevance of kattes in Bengaluru’s urban design and planning. “We feel that they are a fantastic model of “shared spaces”, given the interdependencies between the religious, social and economic activities, with footfalls from one bringing footfalls to the other,” says Kiran. “We don’t have the resources that the West has, so creating a public space model that is suited to what we have, and our culture makes more sense.”
She, therefore, hopes that this book manages to reach many Bengalureans and people working on urban design, she says. “We need to have an Indian idiom of urban design, and the kattes are a great example.”

stories.headline: Residents challenge railway land markings ahead of demolition in Bengaluru
stories.deck: The affected families in Balaji Layout and Prakruthi Township are challenging the Railways’ claim over the marked portions of their properties, which have been identified in connection with the Bengaluru Suburban Rail Project
stories.bodyText:
The demolition of portions of around 25 houses in Horamavu, earlier scheduled for November 21 following eviction notices issued by the South Western Railway (SWR), has been put on hold after residents approached the court.
The affected families in Balaji Layout and Prakruthi Township are challenging the Railways’ claim over the marked portions of their properties, which have been identified in connection with the Bengaluru Suburban Rail Project.
Rail Infrastructure Development Company (Karnataka) Limited (K-RIDE), which is executing the suburban rail project, has identified properties required along the proposed alignment. Private land required for the project is to be acquired through the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board (KIADB), with compensation paid to the owners, before being made available for the project. In Horamavu, railway authorities have marked portions measuring between six and 12 metres from the edge of the Horamavu Railway Under Bridge compound. The SWR Estate Office then issued eviction notices to around 25 households, treating the marked portions as encroachments on railway land. This has led to uproar among the residents, who questioned the basis of the demolition.
A.V. Antao, who has been living in the locality since 2003, said the authorities had not provided documents to establish their claim over the properties or survey maps showing the exact extent of land being claimed. Despite submitting sale deeds, e-Khatas and tax receipts, residents are yet to receive the corresponding land records from the Railways to substantiate its claim.
The residents also argue that there is no explanation given on how these 25 houses were selected, as they point out that apartment complexes in the area are not served on the notices.
Long time residents like Mohammed Ismail, have also cited earlier cases involving railway land claims in Horamavu. In April 2023, the Additional City Civil and Sessions Court in Bengaluru set aside eviction orders issued by the SWR Estate Officer in several appeals. The residents argue that the court then found that the Railways had not produced sufficient material to establish its claim over the disputed properties. The court held that questions of ownership could not be decided through summary eviction proceedings before the Estate Officer and set aside the eviction orders. The residents allege that the notices have been now served in similar manner again, further arguing that they had not been conducted in the presence of the affected property owners.
Residents say they are not opposed to land being taken for the suburban rail project but want the authorities to establish ownership and clearly demarcate the portions required. If the land is privately owned and needed for the project, they demanded that it acquired through the prescribed process with compensation.

briefs.headline: Former gram panchayat official of Bengaluru gets 6 years in jail, fined entire Rs 92 lakh worth of disproportionate assets
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 A special court for Lokayukta cases has sentenced a former gram panchayat (GP) secretary to six years of simple imprisonment for amassing unexplained wealth of Rs 92 lakh during nearly 18 years of public service.
A Veeregowda, who had served as secretary of Rajanukunte gram panchayat (GP) in Bengaluru North taluk and later at Mandur GP in Bengaluru East taluk, has also been fined the entire worth of the disproportionate assets.
In case of default, he will have to undergo an additional year in prison. Veeregowda, who was present in court when the order was pronounced, was taken into judicial custody and shifted to Bengaluru Central Prison. Lokayukta police said he would have to pay the fine before filing an appeal against the order.
Special judge CM Pushpalatha held that Veeregowda had failed to satisfactorily explain the source of assets acquired by him and his family during the period from June 30, 1990, to Dec 18, 2008. R Badrinath, public prosecutor, argued the case for Lokayukta Bengaluru city division. The case had been registered in 2008. The investigation found several movable and immovable assets held in the names of Veeregowda and his wife, 
Bhavya
.
During the trial, Veeregowda argued that the assets did not belong exclusively to him but were part of a large joint family’s holdings. He claimed that the family earned income from agriculture, dairy farming, brick manufacturing, real estate transactions and his wife’s business, Meghana Enterprises.
He also claimed that the gold and silver articles recovered during the investigation were gifts received at marriages and family functions, that some vehicles were used by his brothers, and that several expenses had been met from joint family funds.
The court, however, rejected several of these explanations for want of documentary evidence.
One of the claims related to Rs 13.1 lakh that Veeregowda attributed to his wife’s income from a saree business, Sri Chowdeshwari Silks and Sarees. The court found that the business was registered in the name of AN Rajanna, not Bhavya. The defence did not produce a licence, accounts or bank statements to establish that Bhavya ran the business. Neither Bhavya nor Rajanna was examined to support the claim.
The court also rejected the claim that agriculture and sericulture had generated substantial income for the family.
It said revenue records alone could not establish actual cultivation, yield or earnings. The prosecution produced a communication from the sericulture department stating that neither Veeregowda nor his family members were registered sericulture farmers or had undertaken recognised sericulture activities during the relevant period.
It observed that merely claiming that expenses were met from joint family income was insufficient without bank records, account books, receipts or other evidence showing the source and use of the money. The court also noted that Veeregowda had already received his separate share in the joint family properties and could not rely on joint family funds to explain his personal expenditure without supporting evidence.
Inset - 1
Court’s own assessment
Lokayukta had initially calculated the disproportionate assets at Rs 94 lakh. However, after examining the evidence and considering the defence objections, the court revised the figures. It accepted legitimate income of Rs 40.3 lakh, assets of Rs 69.5 lakh and expenditure of Rs 63 lakh. This meant the unexplained wealth was Rs 92 lakh.

briefs.headline: After Rs 14/kg hike, Karnataka Milk Federation cuts Nandini curd price by Rs 2/kg; households, hoteliers cry foul
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: For consumers still reeling from the steep hike in dairy prices earlier this month, the 
Karnataka
 Co-operative Milk Producers’ Federation Ltd (KMF) has offered a modest reprieve, announcing a Rs 2 per kg reduction in the retail price of Nandini curd from Sunday (Nov 29).
The rollback follows a directive from chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
, who faced considerable backlash over the steep hike in milk and curd prices announced four weeks ago. Under the revised pricing structure, the cost of a 1 kg pouch of Nandini curd will come down from Rs 68 to Rs 66, while the price of the 500 g pouch will be reduced by Re 1, from Rs 34 to Rs 33.
However, the modest reduction has done little to appease consumers, particularly those in the hotel industry, who have dismissed it as a token gesture. Despite KMF’s projection of the move as consumer relief, households and commercial establishments will continue to pay Rs 12 more per kg than they did in October — a net price increase of nearly 22.2%. More importantly, milk variants, which witnessed steep hikes of Rs 8 to Rs 12 per litre on Nov 1, remain untouched.
For ordinary households across Bengaluru and the rest of Karnataka, the Rs 2 rollback has triggered frustration rather than relief. 
With milk and curd being indispensable daily staples in South Indian households, consumers argue that a saving of Re 1 or Rs 2 per pouch does little to ease the wider financial burden imposed by the November 1 price revision.
“Raising the price by Rs 14 and then reducing it by Rs 2 is nothing short of an eyewash. A family of four easily consumes a litre of milk and half a kilo of curd every day. Our monthly dairy bill went up by nearly Rs 450 after Nov 1, and this revision will save us barely Rs 30 a month. Meanwhile, toned milk continues to cost Rs 54 per litre and special toned milk Rs 64 per litre. It feels as though the govt is mocking the common man,” said Jayesh, a Jayanagar resident.
The hotel industry, among the largest bulk consumers of Nandini milk and curd, has also termed the revision inconsequential. Nagendra Kamath, secretary of the Bruhat Bengaluru Hotels Association (BBHA), said the marginal rollback would do little to offset the additional operating costs borne by eateries following the Nov 1 revision.
“Hotels, darshinis and catering units consume hundreds of litres of milk and large quantities of curd every day for coffee, tea, curd rice, lassi and gravies. When KMF increased milk prices by Rs 8 to Rs 12 per litre and curd prices by Rs 14 per kg on November 1, our daily input costs shot up, forcing several small and mid-sized eateries to reluctantly increase the prices of coffee, tea and meals. A Rs 2 reduction in curd prices, with no corresponding cut in milk prices, is negligible and does nothing to restore our margins. Consumers should not expect hotels to reduce menu prices on the back of such a cosmetic rollback,” he said.
KMF had initially justified the Nov 1 price revision, citing severe drought-like conditions, untimely rainfall and escalating costs of green fodder and cattle maintenance for Karnataka’s 8.9 lakh active dairy farmers. However, the steep increase, which pushed curd prices up by as much as 25.93%, triggered widespread public anger and a sharp political backlash. Opposition parties accused the state govt of administrative mismanagement and of passing the financial burden on to working-class and middle-income households.
While KMF’s latest press note maintains that the Rs 2 reduction was ordered “in the interest of consumers”, with the objective of balancing household affordability and farmers’ welfare, critics see it as little more than a damage-control exercise. They argue that the token rollback is aimed at easing political pressure rather than providing any meaningful financial relief to consumers and businesses still grappling with the Nov 1 price shock.

briefs.headline: Forum to launch indefinite strike against school adoption scheme in Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
Demanding the immediate withdrawal of the government school adoption/mentorship scheme and the announcement of an action plan for the comprehensive implementation of the Right to Education (RTE) Act, the Government Schools Development Forum is launching an indefinite protest at Freedom Park in Bengaluru from Thursday.
Stating that education is not an act of charity, the forum pointed out that, through the 86th Constitutional Amendment in 2002, Article 21A was inserted, recognising free and compulsory education for all children up to the age of 14 as a fundamental right. To operationalise this right, the RTE Act, 2009, was enacted.
The forum said that while the Congress-led UPA had enacted the RTE Act, the party is now violating it in the State. “The provision of teachers, infrastructure and quality education, which the government is obligated to ensure, should not be left to the benevolence of private entities through acts of charity or adoption schemes. Handing over government schools to private managements or corporate entities is a dangerous development,” the forum said, demanding that the government immediately abandon the government school adoption scheme.

briefs.headline: Minister sets February deadline for completion of most road works in Bengaluru
briefs.deck: At a review meeting, Krishna Byre Gowda said officials must ensure road works were completed within the stipulated time, as complaints about the condition of roads continued to come in from across the city
briefs.bodyText:
With 553 km of roads asphalted so far out of the 2,875 km taken up for development across Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) jurisdiction, Greater Bengaluru Development Minister Krishna Byre Gowda on Wednesday directed officials to speed up the remaining works and complete most of them by February.
At a review meeting with officials of the five city corporations, Mr. Gowda said the government had allocated funds for road development and that officials must ensure the works were completed within the stipulated time, as complaints about the condition of roads continued to come in from across the city. “The funds have been provided to address these problems and give people lasting relief. The works must be completed quickly,” he said.
The Minister attributed the slow progress of road works in recent months to the monsoon and the rise in bitumen prices, partly due to the situation in the Middle East. With the rainy season over, he directed officials to increase the pace of asphalting. He also said contractors should be called for discussions and additional workers deployed wherever required.
“The government has also taken up white-topping of 88 roads covering 130 km at an estimated cost of ₹2,321 crore. Work is under way on about 120 km, while another 20 to 25 km is awaiting traffic-related permissions,” Mr. Gowda said, pointing out that the work would be taken up in phases to minimise inconvenience to commuters and that stretches where work could proceed should be completed by December.
The Minister also reviewed the development of stormwater drains, with work taken up on about 200 km. He said surveys were being conducted in coordination with land surveyors, specifically in the city’s peripheral areas, to identify stretches where drains were yet to be developed. briefs.headline: Bengaluru-based sari boutique pays homage to MS Subbulakshmi with archival collection
briefs.deck: The great granddaughters of MS Subbulakshmi, Aishwarya and Saundarya, who modelled the saris for Aikyatha, talk about their musical heritage
briefs.bodyText:
Resplendent in a silk sari with her nose pin catching the light and her voice enthralling audiences, MS Subbulakshmi was perhaps the most recognised figure in Indian classical music circles, whether one had a penchant for Carnatic music or not. Popularly known as MS, she was an unwitting style icon whose wardrobe shaped the tastes of women and dictated market trends at a time when saris were not mass produced.
Aikyatha, a silk showroom in Bengaluru has launched Suswaram, an archival collection, recreating seven of her iconic saris and named them after musical notes. And the models showcasing these creations are none other than S Aishwarya and S Saundarya, her great granddaughters.
Carnatic musicians in their own right, the granddaughters of Radha Vishwanathan, were spotted at Aikyatha and its co-founder Yeshwanth Sunku says their conversation veered towards MS Blue, a colour so named by the industry as it was often requested by the singer. “MS would regularly ask for this particular shade of blue in sari stores as it photographed well, especially under the stagelights. I was curious to know if it was exclusive to a particular brand,” says Yeshwanth.
He found the colour had only been recreated by stores as per their designs; it was originally woven by Muthu Chettiar, a weaver from Kancheepuram. Yeshwanth asked MS’ family if they still had the sari, and when he had a chance to see it firsthand, he asked permission to recreate it.
Similar saris were specially woven for MS and Radha, who often performed together. Yeshwanth says he got to examine 22 of them, from which he chose seven to recreate. “I made my choice taking into consideration iconic moments and the events they wore these saris to, as well as weaving specifications.”
For instance, Dha in teal and turmeric is a replica of the sari worn by MS and Radha in the image captured by legendary photographer Avinash Pasricha, while Re in green and violet is a recreation of what MS wore while accepting the Bharat Ratna from then President KR Narayan.
Yeshwanth admits there was a sense of discovery and experimentation in his quest. “The original saris were woven on dobby looms, which are rare today. Besides, there aren’t too many weavers who have the technical know-how to create these pieces.”
He continues, ”Earlier, saris were woven with two colours for the body, and two for the border. I found three weavers who specialised in this craft and got it done. It was only because we had access to the originals that we were able to replicate them exactly.”
Aishwarya says her favourite from the collection is Ga, a creation of blue and red stripes, while Saundarya’s is Re. “As a family, we only have a few saris of my great-grandmother’s; she used to donate a lot of what she had, including the remunerations she received. We were happy to share what we had with Aikyatha,” says Aishwarya.
For both the sisters, the tastefully done photoshoot was a glimpse into MS’ life and the quiet charm of that era. Aishwarya, who was nine at the time of MS’ demise, had attended only two of her concerts. “But I do recall a concert where my grandmother was wearing one of the saris she had while on stage with Ammu Patti (the sisters’ name for MS),” she says.
She continues, “We were quite excited about the saris’ curation; the script for the shoot depicted the saris as a symbol of the culture, music and values passed on to us from Ammu Patti. It was an amazing experience.”
Born a few months after MS passed, Saundarya felt the shoot was a chance to channel all that she had heard about the legend, but never had a chance to be part of. “For a while it was akin to living in an era I would have loved to have been a part of. My grandmother had told me a lot about Ammu Patti and the photos are a peek into the beautiful traditions of those times.”
“Ammu Patti would wear cotton saris and glass bangles at home. We too, wear Kancheevarams for concerts, and Mysore silks or cottons for pujas and family functions; we felt a definite vibe and emotional connect at the shoot,” adds Saundarya.
Needless to say, the original saris are carefully preserved by the family and donned only during special occasions sans safety pins.
Both sisters began their musical training at age four and are busy as musicians today, performing together. “The musical journey of our grandmother and great grandmother was extraordinary, but at the same time, it belongs to a different era. Our intention is not to recreate it, but honor and understand it, and keep it alive in meaningful ways so the next generation can connect with their music, values, and the cultural richness they represented,” says Aishwarya.
“At the same time, we believe it is important to explore new ideas and create experiences that speak for today’s world.”
Saundarya continues, “I believe the greatest thing we can carry forward is their love and support for music. As Carnatic musicians ourselves, we understand how much dedication, discipline, and devotion it requires, and we hope to continue learning, growing, and contributing to this beautiful tradition of melody.”
Set to music
Apart from the Archival Collection, Aikyatha also created a Raga Edition of five saris inspired by the ragas MS was known for.
“MS was known for her rendition of the Shankarabarnam Raga. We have picked up similar ragas and have converted them into saris as an ode to her,” says Yeshwanth, adding that this sari is blue in colour because the raga is in praise of Lord Nataraja who is also known as Nilakantan. “On its border is the bilva leaf which is sacred to Lord Shiva. Other motifs on the body and pallu suggest it is a depiction of the Shankarabarnam Raga.”
“Basically, Kanchivarams are inspired by temple architecture. Sadly, today many saris sport random designs without any structure. This is why we decided to delve into these ragas and converted them into design.”
While only the Shankarabarnam has been released, the others — Saveri, Kalyani, Khamboji and Bhairavi — will be launched shortly with announcements on Aikyatha’s socials.

briefs.headline: Echoes of Earth 2026: The Hills come alive
briefs.deck: Echoes of Earth, Bengaluru’s sustainable music festival, turns 10 this year and is moving to a newer, bigger location
briefs.bodyText:
Did you know as many as five rivers originate from Nandi Hills, Bengaluru’s favourite drive-to destination? Or that the hill range is older than the Himalayas?
It came as news to Roshan Netalkar, founder of the Echoes of Earth music festival. The homegrown festival turns 10 this year and apart from an interesting line-up to mark the milestone, its venue has changed too, moving to Nandi Hills this time round.
“Our theme this year is Arteries for Life and it revolves around river ecosystems in India. It was during our research on the venue that we came across these amazing facts and figures. We felt the festival would be a great opportunity to talk about Nandi Hills,” says Roshan.
The location may have changed, but Roshan stresses there has been no let up in “our commitment to sustainability, conservation or our music lineup. The festival is based on an innovation platform, so every time it feels as though we are doing something new. There has been no chance for monotony or fatigue to set in even though we host the festival year after year.”
With concert goers flocking in from Mumbai, Delhi, Dubai, Sri Lanka and other places, Roshan says the hope is for Echoes to become a destination festival, “where people come in, meet their friends and loved ones, stay at a place together and enjoy a two-day event”.
There is a lot of “muscle memory” associated with the festival for both visitors and organisers in terms of location, he adds. “With the shift in location it is a new canvas, and exploration will be a big part of Echoes this year. People will discover more art, great food and more as the festival will be spread over 125 acres.”
The Greener Side is the initiative that works on Echoes’ aspects of circularity, conservation, and sustainability throughout the year. With the festival celebrating the rivers of India, its water bodies, and the ecosystems that exist within that space, Shreya Chopra, community manager, The Greener Side by Echoes of Earth, says, “A lot of water goes into the production of denim and electronic items. For instance, creating a pair of jeans utilises about 3,000 litres of water, while a smartphone consumes 18,000-20,000 litres of water in its production, enough to meet the drinking water needs of many people.”
“The concert lasts for two days, but we try to engage with the community on the subject of sustainablity through the year by partnering with third-party spaces,” she says.
This year, they partnered with 1,522 outlets where people could drop off their e-waste and denim. “Bengaluru’s active pub scene sees a lot of community activity. We wanted to make it easier for people to head to their nearest watering hole after work and leave their contributions.”
Shreya says these drives are timed around the festive season when people are cleaning out their closets and considering new purchases. “We incentivise these contributions and over the past three years, the number of people wanting to contribute in some way or the other, even after the festival has concluded, has increased.”
This year’s waste collection drive rounded up around 916.5 kilos of e-waste and 335 kilos of textile waste that would have ended up in landfills. That apart, 924 kilos of e-waste and 341 kilos of denim were also sourced from the drive at Bangalore International Airport.
Almost all the e-waste that is collected is utilised at the festival by artists working on installations, Shreya
Echoes’ lineup for this year will feature Fish56Octagon, Elvis Lobo, Ranjit Arapurakal, the Tamil Jazz Collective, Hashbass, Film B2B Rafiki, Kandy Kuri B2B Bombie and Kamari, among others.
Echoes of Earth 2026 will take place on December 5 and 6, at the foothills of Nandi Hills. Tickets and other details on echoesofearth.com
