stories.headline: RBI brings another 60 tonnes of gold home; 84% reserves now held in India
stories.deck: According to the RBI's latest half-yearly report, India's gold reserves stood at 880.52 metric tonnes at the end of September. Of this, 740.13 metric tonnes, equivalent to 84% of the total, were held within the country. The remaining 140.39 metric tonnes were kept with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements.
stories.bodyText:
The 
Reserve Bank of India
 (RBI) has been bringing back India’s gold stored abroad for some time now and it continued to shift the yellow metal reserves back even in this year.
However, what is interesting to note is that gold accounted for a smaller proportion of the country's overall foreign exchange reserves at the end of September, data released on Wednesday showed.
Despite the increase in gold held within India, its share in total foreign exchange reserves fell to 14.38% at the end of September, compared with 16.7% six months earlier.
RBI moves back most of India’s gold reserves
According to the RBI's latest half-yearly report, India's gold reserves stood at 880.52 metric tonnes at the end of September. Of this, 740.13 metric tonnes, equivalent to 84% of the total, were held within the country.
The remaining 140.39 metric tonnes were kept with the Bank of England and the Bank for International Settlements.
RBI repatriated around 60 tonnes of gold during April-September 2026. India has been progressively repatriating its gold holdings over the past two years amid rising geopolitical risks. In March, 77% of the country's gold reserves were held domestically.
India’s forex reserves
India's foreign exchange reserves totalled $705.3 billion, according to the latest data released by the central bank on Friday.
When reserves stood at $668.6 billion at the end of June, they were sufficient to cover 9.8 months of imports, the RBI said.
The ratio of short-term debt to foreign exchange reserves climbed to 23% at the end of June 2026, up from 21.6% at the end of March. The ratio of volatile capital flows, including portfolio investments, to reserves also increased, reaching 68% at the end of June against 66.6% three months earlier.
Most of India's foreign exchange reserves continue to be invested in securities issued by overseas governments. In addition, $35.95 billion was held as deposits with other central banks and the Bank for International Settlements, while $42.75 billion was deposited with commercial banks abroad.
"With the objective of exploring new strategies and products in reserve management while diversifying the portfolio, a small portion of the reserves is being managed by external asset managers," the RBI said.
The period was marked by heightened geopolitical uncertainty, driven by the conflict in West Asia, interruptions to energy supplies and tighter monetary policies adopted by several major central banks.
Global gold prices fell by around 9%, with the average price dropping from $4,721 per troy ounce in April 2026 to $4,319 in September.
"Prices responded to rising US Treasury yields, a stronger US dollar and expectations of tighter monetary policy. The decline occurred despite continued investor demand for gold as a safe-haven and for portfolio diversification," the report noted.
India's overall foreign exchange reserves, meanwhile, grew by $46.67 billion during April-September 2026. They increased from $691.11 billion at the end of March to $737.78 billion at the end of September.
Of the $608.26 billion in foreign currency assets held at the end of September, $529.57 billion was invested in securities. A further $35.95 billion was placed with other central banks and the BIS, while $42.75 billion was maintained as deposits with commercial banks overseas.
The report also pointed to shifts in the composition of global foreign exchange reserves. The US dollar's share fell from 57.18% in the first quarter of 2026 to 56.70% in the second quarter. Over the same period, the euro's share rose from 20.04% to 20.60%.
The RBI reiterated that protecting the safety of India's foreign exchange reserves and ensuring their liquidity remain the central priorities in managing the portfolio, with returns optimised within these parameters.

briefs.headline: IRDAI health panel forms 2 study groups to enhance transparency in claims
briefs.deck: The formation of the two groups by the IAC (Insurance Advisory Committee) Sub-Committee on Health Insurance comes in the backdrop of expanding health insurance coverage.
briefs.bodyText:
Insurance regulator IRDAI has announced the setting up two study groups to recommend measures to enhance transparency and strengthen accountability in health insurance claims.
The formation of the two groups by the IAC (Insurance Advisory Committee) Sub-Committee on Health Insurance comes in the backdrop of expanding health insurance coverage and how standardised metrics and real-time visibility of the claims journey can facilitate performance assessment, strengthen accountability and improve policyholder confidence, the regulator said.
The study groups will recommend standardised claims and grievance metrics, a common framework for claim related reason codes and real time visibility of the claims process, which in turn are expected to improve transparency and accountability. Both groups will be chaired by IRDAI Executive Director Ayyaj Tamboli and comprise representatives from general and health insurance companies, third party administrators, the Insurance Information Bureau of India, the Asian Development Bank and World Bank, thus bringing regulatory, industry and international expertise to examine the issue and “develop practical recommendations.”
The first study group will develop outcome-oriented claims and grievance metrics covering key indicators such as Paid-to-Claimed Ratio, settlement and rejection rates, partial settlements (disallowances), average deductions, cashless utilisation and claims turnaround times. It will also propose a common national code framework for claim rejections, repudiations, deductions and partial settlements, including mapping of existing insurer and TPA codes. The framework will seek to ensure that every rejection or deduction is supported by a specified reason and the corresponding amount affected, thereby enhancing transparency in claim decisions.
The second study group will recommend a mechanism to provide policyholders and other stakeholders with real-time visibility of the standardised health insurance claims journey, from pre-authorisation to final settlement or payment. It will examine the existing communication processes and also define the information to be made available at each stage, including claim status, pending requirements, action required and the party responsible for the next action, along with appropriate modes of communication to keep policyholders informed.
It will also recommend an implementation framework, including a pilot involving select insurers, TPAs and hospitals, followed by phased adoption across the industry. December 26 is the deadline for both the groups to submit their reports, IRDAI said in a release on Tuesday.

SpaceX
 to deploy up to 1 million 
satellites
 that will function as data centres in space, as the company seeks to meet rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing.
The FCC said on Wednesday it had approved SpaceX's proposed "Starmind" constellation of orbital computing modules which would process massive amounts of data and transmit it back to Earth.
SpaceX had earlier sought permission to deploy up to 1 million satellites to support AI computing infrastructure in space.
The FCC said the approval would allow SpaceX "to pioneer emergent technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence".
Data centres are the physical backbone of artificial intelligence, requiring enormous amounts of electricity to run and cool computing systems.
SpaceX has proposed powering its orbital data centres using solar energy, arguing that the technology could significantly reduce energy costs and the environmental impact associated with conventional data centres on Earth.
"By directly harnessing near-constant solar power with little operating or maintenance costs, these satellites will achieve transformative cost and energy efficiency while significantly reducing the environmental impact associated with terrestrial data centers," SpaceX told the FCC.
The company plans to use its next-generation Starship rocket which is currently under development to deploy the constellation.
The ambitious proposal depends heavily on Starship's ability to lower launch costs and carry large numbers of satellites into orbit.
FCC chairman Brendan Carr said the approval would help the US strengthen its position in artificial intelligence and expand computing infrastructure.
"America is leading the world into the era of super intelligence. Under President Trump's leadership, the United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people. The FCC supercharges that effort today by granting, for the first time ever, authorization to deploy 1 million orbital compute modules for data centers in space. This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth," Carr said.
"Compute campuses or data centers are essential to sustaining America’s leadership in SI. By moving compute capacity beyond Earth, SpaceX and the many competitors working on their own orbital data centers are meeting the moment. This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," he added.
The FCC has also approved SpaceX's request to establish backup communications for its optical network. The system will use radiofrequency links for emergency telemetry, tracking and command operations, as well as backup connectivity across the satellite network.
The approval allows communications in the 18.8–19.3 GHz bands for downlinks and 28.6–29.1 GHz bands for uplinks.
It remains unclear whether SpaceX will eventually deploy the entire constellation. There are currently around 17,000 satellites in orbit, and deploying 1 million would represent an unprecedented expansion of satellite infrastructure, Reuters reported.
Satellite operators often seek approval for larger constellations than they ultimately intend to deploy, allowing flexibility as their technology and business plans evolve.
SpaceX had previously sought approval for 42,000 Starlink satellites. The network currently has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.
Amazon's satellite unit Leo and other competitors have questioned SpaceX's proposed constellation arguing that deploying the entire network could take centuries and that the company may not launch all the satellites it has sought approval for.
Carr dismissed the criticism in March, saying, "Amazon should focus on getting Amazon's house in order with their own launches and their own satellite constellation, rather than worrying about other people that are actually out there launching satellites at the pace and cadence that SpaceX is."
Under the approval, SpaceX must begin deployment by November 2033 and launch at least 10% of the approved constellation, or 100,000 satellites by November 2035 and deploy 50% by November 2038.

briefs.headline: Travel pushes LRS remittances past $3bn in September
briefs.deck: In September, the Liberalised Remittance Scheme witnessed a remarkable increase in outward remittances, reaching a 24-month record of $3.2 billion. The primary catalyst was a 21% rise in travel expenditures. Concurrently, both equity and debt instrument investments contributed to this growth. However, there was a downturn in remittances for education and medical expenses abroad, indicating a…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Outward remittances under the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS) rose 15% month-on-month to a 24-month high of $3.2 billion in Sept, from $2.7 billion in Aug, driven largely by higher spending on overseas travel. Remittances for travel increased 21% to almost $2 billion from $1.6 billion, accounting for nearly 84% of the overall increase in outward remittances during the month.
The remittances had last crossed $3 billion in Aug 2024. The average monthly remittance in FY26 was $2.4 billion with most spending in the travel category.
There was also an increase in remittances for investment in equity and debt instruments, which rose 13% to $363 million from $322 million. Transfers as gifts increased 15% to $247 million, while remittances for maintaining close relatives overseas rose 13% to $311 million. Deposits and purchases of overseas property also recorded increases. The rise in these categories was partly offset by a decline in remittances for studies abroad, which fell 29% to $136.5 million from $191.8 million. Remittances for medical treatment also declined to $3.7 million from $4.8 million. Overall, the Sept increase was primarily travel-led, with higher overseas investment, gifts and family maintenance transfers providing additional support.

briefs.headline: RBI flags rising inflation, says economist on firm footing
briefs.deck: In October, India’s economy showcased impressive resilience, bolstered by heightened consumption and credit activities. However, retail inflation climbed to 6.1%, eclipsing the RBI's target as multiple sectors faced price hikes. Eleven states noted inflation rates above 6%, indicating extensive financial strain beyond just food items. Amidst this, GST collections soared to near-record heights…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: India’s economy outperformed major economies in Oct, driven by consumption, credit, industry and exports. Inflation, however, broadened beyond food to fuel, clothing, housing, healthcare and services, with 
RBI
’s Nov State of the Economy report flagging rising price pressures alongside resilient growth, raising expectations of a rate hike.
Retail inflation rose to 6.1 per cent in Oct from 5.5 per cent in Sept, breaching RBI’s 6 per cent upper tolerance limit for the first time since Oct 2024. Inflation above 4 per cent and 6 per cent spread across more CPI items and regions, with urban inflation at 5.4 per cent, rural at 6.6 per cent and food inflation at 8.2 per cent and 8.7 per cent, respectively. Eleven states and UTs recorded inflation above 6 per cent.
Fuel inflation rose to 5.5 per cent, core inflation to 4.5 per cent and core inflation excluding precious metals to 3.8 per cent.
Festive demand lifted GST collections by 22.9 per cent to the second-highest monthly level since the tax’s launch, while e-way bills hit a record, up 23.1 per cent. Electricity demand, diesel consumption, toll collections and digital payment value rose 21.9 per cent, 12 per cent, 12.3 per cent and 22.9 per cent, respectively. Credit demand remained strong, while reserve money and currency in circulation grew at their fastest pace in over five years. Unemployment eased to 4.9 per cent from 5 per cent in Sept.

briefs.headline: Abrupt end to Kalyan-raj at Flipkart
briefs.deck: On December 4, Kalyan Krishnamurthy will step down as CEO of Flipkart after nearly a decade, following clashes with Walmart over financial and listing strategies. An emergency town hall disclosed the unexpected changes, leaving senior executives stunned. Krishnamurthy's leadership had revitalized Flipkart, yet Walmart's focus remains on bolstering financial stability pre-IPO. In the temporary…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: 
Flipkart
 group CEO Kalyan Krishnamurthy, who helped turn around the homegrown 
e-commerce
 major when it was losing ground to Amazon, is leaving after nearly a decade at the helm, amid differences with parent Walmart over listing plans and financial priorities.
Krishnamurthy’s last working day will be Dec 4, just nine days after the announcement, according to an internal communication from Walmart International president and CEO Chris Nicholas to employees, reviewed by TOI. An emergency town hall was called on Wednesday, with the news of an abrupt leadership transition at one of India’s most valuable internet companies catching even senior leadership off guard.
“Most of us were clueless. It’s so sudden since tension, if any, was not apparent,” a senior Flipkart executive told TOI.
Sources in the know claimed Krishnamurthy and Walmart’s leadership differed over the timing of Flipkart’s public listing and providing liquidity to employees holding stock options. While an initial public offering (
IPO
) had been in the works for some time, Walmart has been pushing the company to improve its financial performance before going public.
Chief product and technology officer Balaji Thiagarajan and the Flipkart board will lead the company in the interim. 
A successor will be announced in the coming weeks.
Krishnamurthy’s association with Flipkart goes back nearly 15 years, when he left eBay to join Tiger Global, a key investor in the company. He served as Flipkart’s interim CFO in 2013-14 before returning to Tiger.
His return in mid-2016 came during the most difficult period in Flipkart’s history. Sales growth had stagnated, repeated valuation markdowns hurt investor sentiment, senior executives were leaving and Amazon had committed $5 billion to India.
Focusing on smartphones, large appliances and branded fashion, Krishnamurthy helped Flipkart regain market share, demonstrating an Indian startup could hold its own against a global giant. Co-founder Binny Bansal had replaced Sachin Bansal as CEO in 2016.

briefs.headline: 85-year-old wins case to evict son and daughter-in-law from Delhi home
briefs.deck: An elderly man owns a flat which he acquired from the Delhi Development Authority in 1980 and converted it into freehold in 2000. His eldest son and daughter-in-law had been living there since their marriage in 2003. The Delhi High Court noted that the father's ownership was undisputed. The son and daughter-in-law had not claimed ownership rights over the property.
briefs.bodyText:
Can children forcefully continue to live in their parents’ self-acquired property if the latter ask them to vacate? An 85-year-old man has secured relief with the Delhi High Court asking his son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property.
The court held that a senior citizen seeking eviction under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, does not necessarily have to prove that his children have ill-treated him.
What the case is about
An elderly man owns a flat which he acquired from the Delhi Development Authority in 1980 and converted it into freehold in 2000. His eldest son and daughter-in-law had been living there since their marriage in 2003.
The man claimed that he had asked the couple to arrange alternative accommodation after his second son married in 2005 and his youngest son married in 2008. He alleged that the couple refused to leave, that their behaviour towards him deteriorated over the years and that they stopped supporting him financially. He further claimed that their harassment intensified after his wife died in November 2020.
The father alleged that in 2022, the couple threatened him and assaulted his youngest son. 
He said he filed a police complaint and subsequently approached the authorities under the 2007 Act, seeking eviction and maintenance.
The District Magistrate rejected his application in 2023, observing that the allegations had not been proved and that the Act was being used to resolve a business dispute between the sons.
The father appealed and in June 2025, the Divisional Commissioner set aside the original order and sent the matter back for reconsideration because the first inquiry had not determined whether the complaint was genuine.
A fresh enquiry report again concluded that harassment had not been established. The District Magistrate rejected the application and the Divisional Commissioner upheld that decision in April 2026.
The father then approached the Delhi High Court. His counsel argued that, as the property's absolute owner, he was entitled to live there peacefully and that proof of ill-treatment was not a prerequisite for eviction.
The respondents disputed his account. Their counsel argued that the complaint had been made at the instance of the father's younger son amid a business dispute between the brothers. They also maintained that they had been looking after the father and had offered to pay him Rs 15,000 a month as maintenance.
Why Delhi High Court asked son & daughter to vacate
The Delhi High Court noted that the father's ownership was undisputed. The son and daughter-in-law had not claimed ownership rights over the property and were living there because of their relationship with him. The father had also made it clear that he no longer wished to share his home with them.
The court relied on the Supreme Court's August 4, 2026, decision in 
Ravi Kant Gupta v. State of Uttar Pradesh & Ors.
, which recognised that tribunals under the Senior Citizens Act could order eviction where necessary to protect a senior citizen.
It also referred to the Delhi High Court's earlier ruling in 
Pritam Singh v. Government of NCT of Delhi & Ors.
, which recognised that proof of ill-treatment was not invariably necessary if the property needed protection so the senior citizen could live peacefully.
The court found that the authorities had made proof of harassment an essential condition without considering whether the property needed protection.
It criticised the first enquiry report for being inconclusive, observing: “A report which is, on its own showing, inconclusive could not have formed the basis of a finding that the allegations of harassment stood disproved.”
The authorities had also failed to adequately consider the father's repeated police complaints and an earlier High Court direction requiring the police to assist him against any threat from the respondents.
The existence of a business dispute between the brothers, the court said, could not by itself justify rejecting the father's grievance.
As the judgment put it: “Merely because there may also exist a business dispute between the sons of the petitioner, the same, by itself, cannot be a ground to hold that the grievance of the petitioner is not genuine, or to deny him the protection afforded under the Act.”
Ultimately, the High Court held that an elderly parent should not be compelled to share his home against his wishes when the relationship has deteriorated to the point of prolonged litigation.
The Delhi High Court observed: “At the age of 85 years, the petitioner is entitled to live in his own house peacefully and with dignity.”
The court set aside the Divisional Commissioner's order and the District Magistrate's order. It directed the son and daughter-in-law to vacate the property within four weeks and instructed the concerned Station House Officer to provide the necessary assistance if required.
Adnan Siddiqui, Partner at King Stubb & Kasiva, told ET that father prevailed before the Delhi High Court because he is the absolute owner of the DDA flat.
Neither his son nor his daughter-in-law has any independent interest in the property, as they were permitted to live there only with his consent. After the father decided that they could no longer stay in the flat because of the harassment he had faced, the Delhi High Court upheld his decision.
Siddiqui says: "This case is significant as it highlights that, in addition to aspects relating to property, the entitlement of older people to live in their own home is also associated with their safety, and both mental and physical wellbeing."

briefs.headline: Lakshmi Venu moves Madras high court for partition of family assets
briefs.deck: Lakshmi Venu has filed a petition in the Madras High Court seeking a division of her family's assets, asserting that efforts to amicably settle matters with her father, Venu Srinivasan, have proven unsuccessful. She is requesting access to documents concerning their joint family assets, emphasizing her knowledge of the Hindu Succession Act. Supported by her mother, Lakshmi champions the need for…
briefs.bodyText:
CHENNAI: Lakshmi Venu, daughter of Venu Srinivasan, has filed a suit before Madras HC seeking partition of the joint family assets of the Venu Srinivasan branch of the TVS family and allotment of her share in them, claiming efforts to reach an amicable settlement have failed.
The suit follows a partition notice she sent to her father, Venu Srinivasan, on Nov 16, asking him, as head of the family, to discharge his fiduciary duties and ensure a fair and lawful division of the assets.
Venu Srinivasan’s response reflected no change in his position, according to a statement issued on her behalf. Lakshmi has also sought the court’s intervention to obtain documents and information that she alleges have been withheld despite repeated requests.
Lakshmi compelled to approach court: Mallika
The suit concerns the ownership and division of joint family assets and does not seek to interfere with the operations of any company, the statement said. Lakshmi has an interest in the continued strength of the businesses and believes any division of assets can be implemented in an orderly manner in accordance with the law.
Supporting her claim, her mother, Mallika Srinivasan, said Lakshmi had been compelled to approach the court after the response to her notice failed to recognise her rights and no progress has been made towards amicable resolution. 
“As a mother, to me, a son and daughter are equal in every respect,” she said.
Lakshmi Venu’s claim is based on her interpretation of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, as amended in 2005, which recognises daughters’ rights in coparcenary property. The assets she seeks to partition include interests held through the VS Trust and other holding entities in businesses such as TVS Holdings, TVS Motor Company, TVS Credit Services and Sundaram-Clayton, allocated to the Venu Srinivasan branch under the 2020 TVS Group family arrangement.
She contends the arrangement did not constitute a partition within her immediate family and that no division or settlement of its assets has been initiated or concluded.

stories.headline: India coach nearly falls off chair as Pant turns 'Stan Stan', plays local cricket
stories.deck: Pant, 29, is one of the leading six-hitters in Test cricket history. He has hit 108 sixes in 53 matches, the second-highest tally in the format.
stories.bodyText:
India wicketkeeper-batter 
Rishabh Pant
 took part in a local cricket match in Christchurch on Wednesday, using the opportunity to to keep his eye sharp ahead of the second New Zealand Test starting Friday.
Pant, 29, is one of the leading six-hitters in Test cricket history. He has hit 108 sixes in 53 matches, the second-highest tally in the format.
Six of those sixes came in the first Test in Wellington last week, where his 128 off 153 balls helped India post a record total of 720/9 in New Zealand. The match ended in a draw.
Pant's appearance in a local Last Man Stands match came after he was spotted in central Christchurch.
One team, Open House Swingers, were down a player and asked Pant if he would fill in, with the Indian star wasting no time picking up the bat to give them a boost.
He turned out for the Open House Swingers against The Chosen Ones at Hagley Park. The venue is next to Hagley Oval, where he will represent India in the second Test.
Listed as Stan Stan on the scorecard, Pant scored 54 off 21 balls, continuing his run-scoring form in New Zealand.
"I saw Rishabh going around on an electric bike," Open House Swingers player Mohammad Safi told the New Zealand Herald.
"So I went and stopped him, and we start talking and taking a few photos and stuff, and I asked him, do you want to play cricket for us?
"He was like, OK, I'll come and play for you guys. Then he came and padded up, went batting, and smashed a few sixes."
India bowling coach 
Morne Morkel
 said he "nearly fell off my chair last night when I saw that".
New Zealand captain Tom Latham described Pant's performance as "brilliant".
"He's obviously a real character of the game is Rishabh, so it's great for him to give his experience back to the LMS teams."
Safi told the New Zealand Herald that the opposition players did not recognise Pant, who was wearing a blue tracksuit. He also said Pant had used his cousin's bat during the match.
"He was asking me to basically give him a single and stuff. Obviously, I was smashing longer sixes than him, and then he was like, give me a turn, let me show you how to hit it," Safi said.
The Open House Swingers won the match by 16 runs.
India's second Test against New Zealand begins on Friday at Hagley Oval.

stories.headline: IND vs NZ second Test: Morne Morkel urges patience with Anshul Kamboj’s performance
stories.deck: At Wellington as innings progressed, Kamboj’s pace dipped prompting questions about his effectiveness on surfaces offering little assistance
stories.bodyText:
Anshul Kamboj may have had an underwhelming start to his Test career, but India bowling coach Morne Morkel has urged patience with the young fast bowler, insisting that it would be premature to pass judgement after just two Tests on largely unresponsive surfaces.
Kamboj, who made his debut during the England tour last year, returned figures of one for 89 at Old Trafford. In Wellington, he picked up an early wicket, contributed a brisk 38 as nightwatcher and bowled with discipline on the final day. However, his pace dipped as the innings progressed, prompting questions about his effectiveness on surfaces offering little assistance.
“It was not just him; look at the New Zealand side, the speeds on that surface were down. You can’t judge somebody from his debut Test as well. There are a lot of emotions, a lot of things going into playing your first Test match,” Morkel said here on Thursday, ahead of India’s second Test against New Zealand.
“Let’s rather support the guy who is doing a hard job, pulling hard overs for the team. Let’s give him a proper run, let him play a couple of games first, and then we can have a discussion.”
With India looking to bounce back in the second and final Test against New Zealand, Morkel also acknowledged that Gurnoor Brar was making a strong case for selection. However, he wants the young pacer to remain focused on being ready rather than getting distracted by the prospect of an opportunity. The six-foot-plus pacer could be an option on the Hagley Oval surface, which has a substantial covering of grass.
“There is a lot of excitement about him since he has joined the Indian team, with his pace and bounce. I think he is a guy who will be well suited to the conditions here,” Morkel said.
“Gurnoor has been knocking on the door. He is doing all the right things. But selection as a player is something that he can’t control. He needs to just make sure he’s ready when he gets the opportunity.”
Morkel, however, does not want India’s pursuit of a victory — and the outside possibility of qualifying for the World Test Championship final — to translate into desperation.
“I don’t like that word ‘desperation’ because then the guys will go out and try too hard and miss their lengths. We need to block out the outside noise and focus on playing our best cricket, taking it session by session,” he said.
“All these guys want to play in that final, and they will give everything possible to make it. But realistically, if we are honest about it, it is going to be a challenge,” he said.

stories.headline: Jaiswal — the all-terrain red-ball machine
stories.deck: The four away Tests right at the start of his career were a great learning experience for him. After his debut in the Caribbean where the pitches played low and slow, those in South Africa were of the exactly opposite kind and opened the young man’s eyes to the challenges that would confront him in the longest format
stories.bodyText:
In the immediacy of defeat at the hands of Australia in the final of the inaugural World Test Championship at The Oval in June 2023, India decided to move on from Cheteshwar Pujara. The irony wasn’t lost on anyone. Pujara had served Indian cricket outstandingly while occupying the No. 3 position in Test cricket, proving to be an able successor to Rahul Dravid and playing influential roles in successive series victories in Australia in 2018-19 and 2020-21.
The irony stemmed from the fact that when India severed ties with Pujara the Test batter, the head coach was Dravid himself.
India’s next assignment after the WTC final loss was a two-Test tour of the Caribbean, originally Dravid’s last Test stint as the head coach. India weren’t scheduled to play another Test match until Boxing Day in Centurion, and Dravid was to bow out after the home 50-over World Cup, which was to end in the middle of November.
Shubman Gill volunteered to drop down to No. 3 to occupy the position left vacant by Pujara’s omission. Skipper Rohit Sharma and Dravid were happy to accommodate that request, which meant they had to find a new opening partner for the captain. That hunt didn’t last long; the duo settled on a 21-year-old left-hander who had left his home in Uttar Pradesh’s Suriyawan more than a decade previously for Mumbai, entirely to pursue his cricketing ambitions.
That wiry, slim left-hander answered to the name of Yashasvi Jaiswal, who had the reputation of being a bit of a dasher. In his time with Mumbai trying to find his feet – a journey that has been chronicled in extensive detail — he had caught the eye of the discerning with his aggression and his daring, but also with his tight defence and largely flawless shot-selection. Jaiswal’s hard work and determination were rewarded with the Test cap in Roseau on July 12, 2023, and what a debut it turned out to be.
Batting as if he were a Test veteran and not someone making his first appearance, Jaiswal impressed with his adaptability and his great patience. R. Ashwin’s off-spin had sent the hosts crashing to 150 all out on the first day, and Jaiswal seemed to take it upon himself to reel in that total all on his own. There were numerous crunching strokes that did his reputation as a go-getter no harm whatsoever, but around those sparkling shots, he showed a wise head on his lean shoulders as he engaged in a terrific partnership with his captain for the first wicket.
Published - November 26, 2026 07:31 am IST

stories.headline: 'He won’t be joining': Jannik Sinner ruled out of Australian Open; here's why
stories.deck: Sinner said on Tuesday that he had undergone a “minor” operation on his right knee after other treatments failed to resolve the problem. He did not provide a timeline for his return to the tour.
stories.bodyText:
Jannik Sinner will miss the Australian Open in January as he continues his recovery from surgery on his right knee, tournament officials confirmed on Thursday.
“We’ve been in regular touch with Jannik’s team and they’ve confirmed he won’t be joining us for the AO in January following his recent surgery,” Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo said in a statement, as quoted by Associated Press.
“Jannik loves competing here in Melbourne and is looking forward to returning for AO 2028. We wish him all the very best with his recovery and look forward to seeing him back on court soon.”
Sinner said on Tuesday that he had undergone a “minor” operation on his right knee after other treatments failed to resolve the problem. He did not provide a timeline for his return to the tour.
The Italian has not played since successfully defending his 
Wimbledon
 title in July, which gave him his fifth Grand Slam singles trophy. He has also lost the world No. 1 ranking to Alexander Zverev.
“I have to respect the protocols at the moment because if we rush things we could have more serious problems,” Sinner said during a news conference in Milan earlier this month.
Sinner had announced the end of his 2026 season last month. A statement from his management team said the 25-year-old Italian “will follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee.”
This will be his second prolonged absence from the tennis tour in two years. In 2025, Sinner accepted a three-month ban as part of a settlement with the World Anti-Doping Agency over a doping case.
Sinner's record at the Australian Open
The Australian Open begins on January 17 at Melbourne Park, where Sinner has won two titles.
He claimed his first Grand Slam singles title by beating Daniil Medvedev in five sets in the 2024 final. He defended the title in 2025, beating Zverev in the final.
Sinner has a 27-5 win-loss record at the Australian Open across seven appearances, giving him an 84% success rate. He lost to Novak Djokovic in the 2026 semifinals.

briefs.headline: 'Gambhir, just look at how he is hitting': WC-winner sends strong message on Sooryavanshi
briefs.deck: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off just 53 balls for India A in the Asia Cup Rising Stars, bringing the debate over his promotion to the senior Indian team back into focus.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: At just 15, Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has already delivered several remarkable batting performances. But his stunning innings against the UAE in the Asia Cup Rising Stars could well be the most special of them all. The youngster went after the bowlers from the start and completely dominated the opposition attack.
Sooryavanshi hammered 204 off just 53 balls for India A in the Asia Cup Rising Stars, bringing the debate over his promotion to the senior Indian team back into focus.
Many former cricketers and experts have backed the youngster for a regular place in India's T20I team. However, his latest knock also underlined his ability to make an impact in the 50-over format.
Former India captain and 1983 World Cup winner Krishnamachari Srikkanth feels the team management must take bold decisions to give Sooryavanshi a bigger role in Indian cricket.
Srikkanth questions Gambhir's approach
Sooryavanshi has featured in 10 T20Is for India but is yet to cement his place in the playing XI. With the full-strength team available, Abhishek Sharma and Sanju Samson have been preferred as openers.
Srikkanth feels the youngster is not getting enough opportunities despite his impressive performances. He also had a strong message for India head coach 
Gautam Gambhir
.
"We need to make some strong moves. Vaibhav was made Bihar captain right away. He was the vice-captain in the Duleep Trophy; him and Ishan (Kishan) won the title. He has been promoted to that level. Gautam is just keeping deaf ears," Srikkanth said, speaking on his YouTube channel.
"The team management is playing one game, saying he has to be groomed, and not giving him chances. This guy, on the other hand, is playing his own game. You say it is not in your hands and all of that. Gautam Gambhir, just look at how he is hitting. No one can hit like this. Just look at this," he added.
'This is another level'
Srikkanth was left stunned by the variety of shots Sooryavanshi played during his remarkable innings. He also praised the youngster's power and timing, saying he had rarely seen anything like it.
"What is this? Have you seen anyone hitting the ball like this? Look at the shots he has played. He has his shots everywhere in all ranges. This is another level. This does not happen in book cricket either. I have never seen these kinds of shots. Who is this guy? Which generation is he from? Where does he get so much power and sense of timing?" he further said.
Srikkanth also compared the 15-year-old's batting to that of some of the biggest hitters in the game, including AB de Villiers and Chris Gayle.
"I have not seen anyone playing like this in a team. Even (AB) De Villiers and (Chris) Gayle did not play like this," Srikkanth concluded.

briefs.headline: Carlos Alcaraz's serve may be a work in progress, but the Spaniard is going places
briefs.deck: The 23-year-old Spaniard defeated world No. 1 Alexander Zverev in straight sets in Sunday’s title match in Turin to claim his first ATP Finals crown. Yet his average first-serve speed was nearly 8 kmph slower than what he had managed in last year’s final against Jannik Sinner.
briefs.bodyText:
Carlos Alcaraz has played six tournaments since returning to competition in August and won four of them, taking his title tally for the year to six. But it is not just the number of titles, or even the fact that his last three triumphs have come on speedy indoor hardcourts - traditionally not the strongest part of his game - that makes this run particularly impressive. It is that he has achieved all this while his serve remains awork in progress.
The 23-year-old Spaniard defeated world No. 1 Alexander Zverev in straight sets in Sunday’s title match in Turin to claim his first ATP Finals crown. Yet his average first-serve speed was nearly 8 kmph slower than what he had managed in last year’s final against Jannik Sinner.
Alcaraz averaged 196 kmph on his first serve and 170 kmph on his second in Turin, although his second-serve speed against Zverev was significantly slower.
Alcaraz, who injured his wrist in Barcelona in April, returned to competition at the US Open in August, where he reached the quarterfinals. Since then, he has won titles in Tokyo, Vienna, Paris and Turin, compiling an impressive 22-1 record in that stretch.
After Sunday’s final, Alcaraz spoke about his grandfather, who reminds him of the three C’s before he steps on court, whether for a match or practice.
“In Spanish it is ‘Cabeza, corazon, cajones’, in English it is ‘head, heart, balls’,” he said in Turin.
While Alcaraz wasted little time rediscovering his forehand after returning to competition, the serve has proved adifferent challenge. The seven-time major champion, who stands at 6ft and, along with Italian Flavio Cobolli, is the shortest player in the ATP’s Top 10, has had to find ways to extract more from his serving action.
There has been a subtle change in his motion since August, including a lift of the front foot that places more weight on the back foot and helps with the loading. He has also lowered his ball toss and quickened his motion. In the superfast indoor conditions in Turin, those adjustments gave his serve an added edge.
“I understand how I should serve, and when I’m relaxed, I do a really smooth movement and I accelerate. When I feel nervous, I want to do more than I should do,” he said. “I’m not (a) server. I need to gain the point from the baseline, so I have to realise that and understand that. Once I got it, I think the serve goes much better.”
Zverev may have finished the year as No. 1, but it is Alcaraz who has given the closing months of the season their most compelling storyline.
He began 2026 under a barrage of questions after parting ways with Juan Carlos Ferrero, the coach who had guided him through his formative years, at the end of a successful 2025 season. The debate over whether the coach made the champion or the genius made the coach has, in many ways, been answered.
Alcaraz has had to fight for his own territory this season, and his response has been emphatic. Ferrero has since signed up to work with 24-year-old world No. 4 Ben Shelton, who dismantled Alcaraz’s challenge at the US Open but has since lost twice to the Spaniard. Their meetings are already being talked up as one of the rivalries to watch in the new season.
For Alcaraz, though, the bigger challenge will be to build on a remarkable finish to 2026. The serve is evolving, but he has shown that he can win on the biggest stages even when one of the most important weapons in his arsenal is not firing at full strength.
If he can combine the improvements in his serve with the fluency of his baseline game, the prospect of an even more formidable Alcaraz in 2027 should concern the rest.

briefs.headline: Batter leaves stumps unattended, gets bowled off 'free ball': What's BBL's weird rule?
briefs.deck: Chasing Heat's total of 137/8, the Renegades were in control at 3-97 before Sarah Glenn dismissed Georgia Wareham. Dottin then walked in but was penalised for taking more than the permitted time to get ready to face the ball.
briefs.bodyText:
Melbourne Renegades survived a scare to keep their Women's Big Bash League (WBBL) campaign alive, beating Brisbane Heat by three wickets in a last-ball finish after Deandra Dottin became the first player to be dismissed under the competition's timed-out rule.
Chasing Heat's total of 137/8, the Renegades were in control at 3-97 before Sarah Glenn dismissed Georgia Wareham. Dottin then walked in but was penalised for taking more than the permitted time to get ready to face the ball.
Under BBL rules, a batter must be ready to face the next delivery within 75 seconds of the previous dismissal. However, the timed-out rule in the competition has an additional provision: the incoming batter must stand to the side while the opposition bowler gets a free delivery at the stumps.
Glenn made the most of the opportunity, hitting the stumps with her free delivery to dismiss Dottin without her facing a ball. The Renegades had slipped from 3-97 to 5-97 in the space of two deliveries.
“This is great drama. Dottin’s out! She was late to the crease and she’s out without facing a ball,” Fox Cricket commentator Corbin Middlemas said. “What a blunder.”
The rule was introduced in the 2021-22 season but had not been enforced before, despite several instances of players taking longer than the permitted time.
Brisbane Heat batter Grace Harris had little sympathy for Dottin, saying professional players should know better.
“No, I haven’t seen it in the game. I know there’s been a rule. If you want some directness. This is professional cricket, not park cricket,” Harris said, as quoted by Fox Cricket.
Despite the setback, the Renegades completed the chase, winning by three wickets off the final ball. Annie Wikman, who remained unbeaten on eight off five balls, guided them home after they needed nine runs from the final over. She had also taken three catches during the Heat innings.
Earlier, 
Sophie Molineux
 took 4-20, dismissing Charli Knott (15) and Harris (0) bowled before claiming two more wickets in three deliveries. The performance also made her the Renegades' all-time leading wicket-taker.
The Heat had recovered from 4-59 to reach 4-90 before Molineux struck again to slow their progress.
The win lifted the Renegades to fourth place in the standings, but they must beat Melbourne Stars on Saturday to secure a place in the finals.

briefs.headline: World Chess Championship: Gukesh, Sindarov sign peace treaty in quick time
briefs.deck: It is all-square in the youngest World title match in history; it is D. Gukesh 1, Javokhir Sindarov 1
briefs.bodyText:
It was London in Geneva on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), a day after Berlin in Geneva.
Editorial | All to play for: on the World chess championship in Geneva
If the first game of the World Chess Championship featuring the Berlin Defence ended in a draw by a repetition, the second game told a similar story: the London System battle took the same route. It is all-square in the youngest World title match in history. It is D. Gukesh 1, Javokhir Sindarov 1.
Game 2 was a much quieter affair, though. Game 1 lasted 38 moves before the two players reached a threefold repetition. It had witnessed some intense chess, and both players were tested by each other. Gukesh’s battle with the clock had also provided some drama.
This time around, Gukesh took a leaf out of his predecessor’s book. He was once again overtaken on the clock by Sindarov. But, the situation wasn’t anywhere as precarious.
Gukesh then chose to bring his dark-squared bishop into action. And it seemed the World champion wanted to bring the London System into another title match. In the previous edition, Gukesh’s rival and the then World champion Ding Liren of China had employed this opening. In that match in Singapore, Ding had, in fact, played the London System twice. And both those games were drawn.
This time around, Gukesh took a leaf out of his predecessor’s book. He was once again overtaken on the clock by Sindarov. But, the situation wasn’t anywhere as precarious.
In the second game, the Grandmaster from Chennai took a lot of time to make his 16th move — ‘f’ pawn push. He had now fallen behind by more than half-an-hour.
Things were pretty even on the board, however, and once Gukesh took his dark-squared bishop to the centre, the chances of a draw looked likely. That was what happened just three moves later.
The 20-year-olds repeated their moves. And this time, Sindarov ensured that he claimed the draw in the proper manner. In the first game, the arbiter had to point out to him that his claim was a bit premature. When the peace treaty was signed in Geneva — how appropriate! — much of the ammunition still remained on the board.
The moves: Gukesh vs. Sindarov: 1. d4 d5 2. Nf3 Nf6 3. Bf4 c5 4. e3 e6 5. Nbd2 Nc6 6. c3 Be7 7. Ne5 Qb6 8. Rb1 Nxe5 9. Bxe5 Bd7 10. a4 O-O 11. Bd3 Qd8 12. O-O Rc8 13. Ra1 Be8 14. Qe2 Nd7 15. Bg3 f5 16. f3 Nf6 17. Be5 17... Nd7 18. Bg3 Nf6 19. Be5 Nd7 20. Bg3 Nf6. Game Drawn.

briefs.headline: India's old nemesis Matt Henry awaits them at his home ground in Christchurch
briefs.deck: From Wellington to Manchester, Bengaluru and, most recently, Mount Maunganui, Matt Henry has inflicted painful wounds. Now, India run into him again at Christchurch’s Hagley Oval, his home ground, in Friday’s second Test, with a series to be won and their last, exceedingly slender World Test Championship hopes still alive.
briefs.bodyText:
Be It Wellington On ODI Debut, Manchester, Mount Maunganui Or Bengaluru, Kiwi Pacer Has Mount Maunganui Or Bengaluru, Kiwi Pacer Has Repeatedly Been The Reason For Indian Heartbreak Repeatedly Been The Reason For Indian Heartbreak
Sometimes, in cricket chronicling, we tend to focus more on stats than impact. Kiwi pacer 
Matt Henry
’s career has been like that. Especially against India. Besides the quartet of Tim Southee, Neil Wagner, Trent Boult and Kyle Jamieson, few New Zealand bowlers of his generation have been as consistent a catalyst for Indian batting debacles across formats as the 34-year-old pacer.
From Wellington to Manchester, Bengaluru and, most recently, Mount Maunganui, Henry has inflicted painful wounds. Now, India run into him again at Christchurch’s Hagley Oval, his home ground, in Friday’s second Test, with a series to be won and their last, exceedingly slender World Test Championship hopes still alive.
Can there be a better setting for Henry?
His international career actually began against India in Wellington in Jan 2014, two years after battling repeated stress fractures in his back. Drafted into the side for the fifth ODI, Henry took 4/38 on debut as New Zealand completed a 4-0 series victory. It was the start of a recurring dream for him and a recurring nightmare for India.
Like Old Trafford. Five years later. In the 2019 World Cup semifinal at Manchester, India were chasing 240 when Henry ripped through their top order in a semifinal stretched over two days due to rain. He had Rohit Sharma, the tournament’s leading run-scorer with five hundreds, caught behind for one before removing KL Rahul. 
Henry finished with 3/37 and the Player of the Match award as India’s World Cup dream ended in an 18-run defeat.
Then came Bengaluru in Oct 2024. On a gloomy morning tailor-made for seam bowling, Henry grabbed 5/15 as India were bundled out for 46, their lowest Test total at home. New Zealand went on to win the Test and, more remarkably, sweep the series 3-0. Henry had delivered the first blow in India’s most deflating home humbling.
And only a fortnight ago, he did it again. At Mount Maunganui, in the fourth ODI, Henry produced the best international figures of his career, 6/27, as India were cleaned up for 89 chasing 334. His opening over was extraordinary: Rohit Sharma, Virat Kohli and Shreyas Iyer were all gone before Ruturaj Gaikwad had even faced a delivery. India were 0/3 after one over and eventually suffered a 244-run defeat.
That is why Henry’s comments about valuing impact over numbers deserve attention. “For me, it is about actually winning games of cricket and winning those moments,” Henry said while addressing the media ahead of the second Test. “As players, you look back, it is probably not the big wicket hauls, but actually the impact you have, and how do you steer a team to win.”
Hagley Oval is Henry’s backyard, the home ground for Canterbury and the venue where his Test career really took off. He has 40 wickets in eight Tests there at 23.32, including two seven-wicket hauls. The first, 7/23 against South Africa in 2022, arrived at a time when Henry’s stop-start Test career seemed to be drifting.
From 2015 to 2021, he had managed only 37 wickets at 46.27, often the fifth option behind Southee, Boult, Wagner and Jamieson. Since 2022, however, he has evolved into one of New Zealand’s premier quicks. In 2024, Henry took 7/67 against Australia at the same venue.
“I suppose it is always nice when you are at home, and it is a ground you have played a lot of cricket at,” Henry said. “You probably have that element of comfort. You kind of know the ground well.”
Hence, he cautioned against assuming it would be a seamer’s delight. “When there is grass on it, wickets tend to get better and better,” he said of New Zealand surfaces. “It is a good batting venue. Obviously, when there is bounce involved, you feel in the game, but from a batting point of view, you can score quickly as well.”
For India, though, the history goes beyond Hagley. Henry’s career has intersected with some of their worst days. It makes Christchurch an ominously appropriate place for another meeting.

briefs.headline: Siraj, Akash Deep or Brar? India face selection dilemma ahead of Christchurch Test
briefs.deck: India went into the Basin Test with four seamers, Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Prasidh Krishna and Anshul Kamboj, and every one of them put in a significant shift, often having to operate into Wellington’s unforgiving wind. Bumrah sent down 49 overs, Kamboj and Prasidh 45 each and Akash 43.
briefs.bodyText:
At around 6.33am India time on Tuesday, three days before the second Test against New Zealand at Hagley Oval in Christchurch, came a terse 13-word WhatsApp alert from the BCCI media team: “Nov 25, 2026 - Christchurch. India. No practice and no press conference. Thank you.”
It was hardly unexpected. With just a three-day turnaround between the two Tests, including a travel day, India were never going to exert themselves immediately after sending down a combined 241 overs across New Zealand’s two innings at the Basin Reserve. The training blocks and practice games are behind them. India will have just one training session, on Thursday, before the second Test, and it is now all about recovery, selection and execution.
India went into the Basin Test with four seamers, Jasprit Bumrah, Akash Deep, Prasidh Krishna and Anshul Kamboj, and every one of them put in a significant shift, often having to operate into Wellington’s unforgiving wind. Bumrah sent down 49 overs, Kamboj and Prasidh 45 each and Akash 43.
After Monday’s dispiriting draw in a Test they had controlled for long periods, skipper Shubman Gill hinted that India may not tinker too much with their XI or, more pertinently, the combination.
There is certainly little in Hagley’s history to encourage them to move away from a paceheavy attack. In the 15 men’s Tests played at the venue, 444 of the 484 wickets have gone to pacers. That’s a massive 91.7%.
So four quicks again? Certainly. But will they be the same four?
India’s batters appear to be in decent touch, with several of them also having had useful time in the middle here during the India ‘A’ game. It is the bowling attack where the more intriguing calls lie.
Could the team management be tempted to hand the nippy Gurnoor Brar a Test debut in place of Anshul Kamboj? Kamboj had a decent outing with bat and ball at the Basin, but when the ball became older and New Zealand’s batters dug in, he appeared a little short of the variations required to keep prising out wickets.
Brar, meanwhile, wasn’t part of the original Test squad. But after being adjudged Player of the Series in the ODIs, he was added to the Test party in place of leftarm wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav.
Can India turn back to the experience and inexhaustible energy of 
Mohammed Siraj
 in place of Akash Deep? That relentless intensity was something India missed at the Basin once the pitch flattened.
The current regime under Gill and coach Gautam Gambhir has prioritised current form and the eye test in the nets. By the looks of it, Siraj hasn’t quite passed that test yet, despite Gill speaking glowingly about him in Wellington.
But if Gill and Gambhir care for history, someone could perhaps point them towards one striking statistic. India have won nine Tests in SENA countries since 2020 and Siraj has featured in every one of them, playing significant roles along the way.
Hagley, like the Basin, has a reputation for rewarding seam, with its grass cover offering the quicks assistance over the first couple of days before batting tends to become easier, particularly under bright skies. The forecast suggests sunshine over the first three days, but considerably more cloud and rain on Days Four and Five. 
That could make having fresh legs in the pace attack even more important.
India were handed first use of the Basin pitch after winning the toss and reduced New Zealand to 70/5. At Hagley, should they win the toss again, expect them to have no hesitation in inserting New Zealand.
History backs that instinct too: in the 15 Tests played here, teams winning the toss and choosing to bowl first have gone on to win nine times.
With valuable World Test Championship points available before New Zealand head across the Tasman to face Australia and India prepare to host Australia for five Tests, both teams will desperately want a result.
